https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.title: Americans, this is your chance to slap down the tech broligarchs
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text:
The midterms will be a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve

“The world should accept some bad things happening,” Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, said recently, “for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” Like so many things tech oligarchs say, it’s incoherent, since Altman would like to deny the world and the people in it the agency to decide whether or not we should accept his bad things. Surveys show that most Americans would like to pause AI; opposition to AI datacenters is a factor in many races in the midterm elections. People are outraged and anxious about what tech hath wrought, mad enough to fight back in what is coming to seem like a human v machine battle.

I’ve been a fan of the film Terminator 2 forever, the one where a badass female protagonist leads the action-movie-style spectacular destruction of Skynet, the massive computer system that will otherwise go rogue and pit itself and a plethora of advanced weapons against the human race. We’re not in a film and we’re probably not going to solve the problems big tech creates through spectacular violence, although the guerrilla campaigns to take down, disable or destroy Flock cameras have some action-movie charms (wading through the bureaucratic process of getting cities to reject or take down the surveillance technology is probably more effective.)

A few months ago, I was surprised to find myself using the term “beautiful hatred” to describe the nationwide revolt against datacenters, Flock cameras, AI, and tech corporations and the oligarchs (or broligarchs) they’ve spawned. It is beautiful because behind fierce opposition to a destructive force is something you’re trying to protect from destruction, something you care about, even love. Behind this revolt against big tech is concern about many things, from the climate to democracy to mental health and humanity itself.

Like the Trump administration, the tech overlords have proceeded on the assumption they can ignore or override the will of the people. The will of the people is in the process of proving them wrong, at least to some extent, and the midterms will be, among other things, a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with predatory tech giants over the public they’re supposed to serve and, arguably, humanity itself. It’s sometimes said only a common enemy can unite a country, and in that sense Silicon Valley has provided something useful at last, because across the political spectrum people hate datacenters and are working to stop them. Datacenterwatch.org reports that at least 142 activist groups across 24 states have organized to block datacenter construction and expansion.

Often the foregrounded concerns are about local issues – effects on land, water, electricity prices, noise – since datacenters offer a lot of negatives and, arguably, no real positives, not even more than a handful of local jobs. But behind that is beautiful hatred of the high-handed efforts to bludgeon communities into accepting something for which they’ll get little in return but trouble – and of AI itself. A nine-year-old I spend time with recently remarked: “I don’t trust AI,” more or less out of the blue, and I think she speaks for a lot of us. Never mind my nine-year-old; the pope is speaking up against it, too, saying in a recent social media post: “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity” and calling on us to “safeguard our humanity” against tech’s incursions.

The tech leaders onstage with Trump at his second inauguration thought they’d turn him into their golden escalator up; the current revolt suggests they could follow him on the golden escalator down. In San Francisco, more than 1,000 nurses and community members came out in a march in September to demand that hospitals cut ties with Palantir, Peter Thiel’s sinister surveillance corporation that also aids Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Nurses in the march noted that the software makes significant errors, violates patient confidentiality and the president of the California Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee said: “The violence and destruction unleashed by immigration agents and enabled by Palantir is a total violation of nursing values of care and compassion.”

Recent news stories, following former Anthropic safety employee Jacob Coxon’s statements about AI’s near-term apocalyptic risks, were further reminders of the absolute amorality of Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. The documents for Anthropic’s IPO acknowledged AI models could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, and the sheer arrogance of choosing to make profit-driven private decisions about the collective future is another reason to loathe and oppose them. Although there are useful and legitimate applications of this technology, the people pushing it on us are pursuing its more dangerous and corrosive uses, even as their products again and again prove harmful and unreliable. In recent weeks another AI safety employee quit, OpenAI’s David Robinson, with a statement noting: “The future depends on wisdom that Silicon Valley lacks.”

We will not see anything as dramatic and decisive as the explosion of Skynet, but we are seeing enough of a grassroots opposition going after so many aspects of tech, that maybe history will remember it as the beginning of our war against the machines. A new organization called Mothers Against Media Addiction (Mama) is going after the effects of the internet and smartphones on children. Other encouraging developments include New York City’s decision to ban AI for students through eighth grade, and the most recent round of lawsuits against Meta for what Instagram and Facebook do to children. Meanwhile congressional Democrats, spurred on by their constituents, are stumbling toward regulation of the tech industry that protects human beings against machines and the owners of those machines.

Another new organization, called the Association for Human Mathematics (AHM), founded in September, declares that it “protects mathematics as a human endeavor against the threat of artificial intelligence”. AHM seems to have been founded in response to OpenAI claiming it solved one of the longstanding problems in mathematics. Since then it has gone after many more, much to the dismay of mathematicians. The mission statement recognizes, as many creative workers do, that the process of thinking, struggling, creating, learning, writing is at least as important as the product, that in doing the work we form ourselves as well as arrive as results. “Why surrender our agency (that amazing ability we have to reach across time and space, with our strange, idiosyncratic phenomenon, and land within the sensibility of another human being) to something that, by its very design, pushes the individual sensibility aside?” said novelist George Saunders of AI.

The spiritually bereft rhetoric of AI, like so much tech rhetoric, insists that doing things is hard and we don’t want to do hard things. As the brilliant tech critic Sherry Turkle points out, AI as currently promoted and used threatens to “deskill” us both intellectually and emotionally, if we depend on it for a sycophantic pandering to our egos in place of the challenge of human relationships, if we make it do our mental labor for us. Like physical strength, emotional and intellectual strength are achieved through efforts tech would like us to abandon in favor of outsourcing the work to their products. A third new anti-AI organization, launched by longtime climate activist Phil Aroneanu, is called Irreplaceable.org, and while its main goal is to regulate AI, its premise is that we need to protect our incomes, our rights, our freedom, but also our humanity against the tech corporations pushing AI.

These new developments point to something that’s going to be important in the resistance to big tech: as it seeks to literally dehumanize us and argues for replacing human beings (and at its most extreme, humanity itself), we must define and cherish and defend what does make us human and what makes being human joyful, meaningful, dignified and honorable. It’s a more nuanced, undramatic job than, say, going after Flock cameras, but not less important. I began this essay talking about beautiful hatred. It is only beautiful if it knows what it opposes because it knows what it loves and endeavors to defend. In this case, we’re defending nearly everything, including democracy, human creativity, human nature and nature itself. Terminator 2’s subtitle is Judgment Day; judgment day in 2026 will be election day, and I’ll be rooting – and voting – for humanity against oligarchical technology.

Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility

Follow them on Substack: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum and Wajahat Ali.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Big business’: little-known court system in Louisiana churns out thousands of evictions – and millions in fees for judges
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Guardian investigation: Louisiana’s justice of the peace court system may violate tenants’ constitutional rights as eviction fees boost judges’ incomes

When she arrived at the justice of the peace court on a rain-soaked morning, Marchana Watts hoped she could fight off her landlord’s push to evict her and her five children from their trailer home on the outskirts of Baton Rouge.

Watts, a careful record keeper who earned $20 an hour as an insurance analyst, came to Justice Tracy Batieste’s small courtroom with receipts. They showed she had paid her $950 monthly rent for the past year and a half, she said.

But when her case was called, Watts said in a complaint to the state judiciary commission, her evidence was “COMPLETELY IGNORED by the ‘judge’. She did not print out all of my documents and didn’t allow me to properly present them.”

Within a few minutes, Watts recalled in a later interview, Batieste moved to the issue of a court fee, instructing the manager of her trailer park to pay up.

He handed the justice a folded bundle of cash with a hundred-dollar bill on top, Watts said. “She stuck it in her robe … And then she was like: ‘You have 24 hours to move.’”

Watts had been evicted from her home by a little-noticed judicial system that orders thousands of evictions in Louisiana each year.

Inside Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts, evictions often move swiftly, landlords rack up wins, some judges earn outsized incomes – and housing advocates say tenants’ fundamental rights are at risk.

The state’s 390 justices of the peace work part-time – ruling on evictions, small claims and wage garnishments as well as, in happier moments, performing weddings. They are required to have only a high school diploma and their courts do not need to keep detailed records or follow standard rules of evidence. They are paid directly by the fees their court charges, including court costs in eviction cases that can total $150 or more.

In court documents and interviews, tenant advocates and legal experts say the interplay between fees and justices’ personal income creates conflicts of interest that can incentivize them to evict tenants and win the favor of landlords who bring in cases and fees.

“Why would landlords prefer to go to a justice of the peace court?” said Bradley Benton, a former legal aid attorney who has defended Louisiana tenants in eviction cases. “It’s faster. It’s cheaper. And it’s easier to evict.”

Eviction fees helped the justice of the peace in one part-time suburban court earn more compensation last year – over $400,000 – than the chief justice of the US supreme court earns.

That justice of the peace is one of five who earned more than $220,000 in a single year from filing fees, much of it derived from eviction cases. Renters are frequently compelled by their leases to pay court costs back to a landlord following evictions.

One longtime justice of the peace calls some of these courts “big business”. A clerk for another justice told a tenant’s lawyer that “we are a for-profit court”. A legal expert described a justice of the peace court in a New Orleans suburb as an “eviction mill”.

The Guardian’s nine-month investigation draws on analysis of more than 11,000 pages of eviction records and 3,400 financial disclosure forms as well as deposition testimony, recently unsealed investigative evidence and documents released under public records requests. The reporting also draws on dozens of interviews with justices, tenants and housing attorneys, and the observation of eviction hearings at five justice of the peace courts in the Baton Rouge and New Orleans metro areas and in St Tammany parish.

“I believe this system is blatantly unconstitutional,” said Lisa Foster, a retired California appeals judge and the former director of the office for access to justice at the US Department of Justice. She pointed to a more than century-old US supreme court precedent, which found that a defendant’s rights were violated if their case was heard before a judge with a direct financial interest in the outcome. “Without question, the Louisiana justice of the peace system has failed its citizens, yet no one seems to be taking action.”

This scrutiny comes as Louisiana’s state government has quietly backed this court system with new laws that expand these justices’ authority, while at the same time passing a law that carries possible jail sentences for homeless people.

In Louisiana and across the US, millions of tenants are struggling as the overall cost of living continues to soar – and rents and junk fees charged on top of rents have surged amid shortages of affordable housing. Roughly one out of every 13 renter households faced eviction filings in 2025, according to research by Princeton University’s eviction lab covering 10 states and dozens of metro areas.

When landlords seek eviction, renters are often at a disadvantage because of their limited finances, lack of understanding of the eviction system and, frequently, lack of legal representation. Studies around the country often show that less than 5% of tenants have lawyers to fight for them in eviction cases, while more than 80% of landlords typically have attorneys on their side.

Uneven playing fields in the eviction process can put additional strains on renters already struggling to get by – piling on court fees, moving charges and other costs and, studies show, harming families’ mental and physical health.

Louisiana, one of the poorest states in the US, offers some of the weakest legal protection for renters in the nation. A first-of-its-kind data analysis conducted by the Guardian found that the eviction filing rate within the jurisdiction of the busiest justice of the peace court was nearly three times the national average. The rate of legal representation for tenants in this court, according to documents reviewed by the Guardian, could be as low as 1%.

The Louisiana Justices of the Peace & Constables Association and the state attorney general’s office did not answer a series of detailed questions from the Guardian for this story.

In a recent public statement, the Louisiana attorney general, Liz Murrill, said the state’s justices of the peace “play a vital role in serving our communities and upholding the rule of law” and “providing access to justice close to home”.

After the short hearing in Justice Batieste’s court concluded in July 2024, Watts left in tears.

She had moved into the three-bedroom trailer home after the death of her sister to be closer to her only remaining sibling. It was cramped and damp. But it was a stable place to live.

The eviction order, tacked to her door earlier in the month, had come as a shock. She had tried to find free legal representation, but Louisiana’s eviction process – which generally requires just 72 hours’ notice before an eviction case can be heard in court – was so fast she did not have enough time.

Black women, like Watts and the majority of renters interviewed for this series, face greater risk of eviction than any other demographic group, according to numerous studies.

Watts said she suspected her eviction was an act of retaliation. Her property manager, who had stood before her in court that day, had made continued, unwanted sexual advances via explicit images sent over text message and knocks at the door past midnight, according to Watts and records seen by the Guardian. In her written complaint – which was part of a tranche of recently unsealed records obtained by the Guardian – she told the state judiciary commission that the manager had “emotionally and mentally abused me”.

Batieste did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Guardian. In an interview with the judiciary commission in February 2025, she asserted that when she ruled on Watts’s case there were “some materials that were missing that kind of had a question mark on them”.

Under state law, Watts had 24 hours to vacate her home. She borrowed money to book a removal van and rent a storage unit to keep her possessions. She found a place for her boys to stay, moving 50 miles south to the rural town of Donaldsonville, which sits on a stretch of the Mississippi River and is surrounded by chemical plants.

For the next four weeks she slept in her car, parked nearby in the driveway of her late grandmother’s abandoned home. She prayed for strength each night before falling asleep in the back seat.

Justice Chuck Cusimano II’s courtroom sits off a tight corridor on the sixth floor of a tall government building in the New Orleans suburb of Harahan. A slight man with wavy gray hair, he has been the elected justice of the peace for Jefferson parish’s fifth district for almost 20 years. He previously served as a district court judge and a state legislator.

Eviction hearings begin promptly at 9.30am on Tuesdays and Thursdays, usually wrapping up before midday. A large clock adorns the left-side wall of the courtroom and wooden public benches are separated by sheets of hard plastic.

On a recent June morning, as the clock ticked a few minutes before 9.30am, a cluster of landlords and property managers lined the benches, waiting to appear before the judge.

“He’ll be done with this whole docket in 30 minutes,” quipped one representative for a local leasing company. “He’s fast!”

The Guardian observed five separate eviction dockets at Cusimano’s court throughout June and July, witnessing the speed with which cases were heard, almost always resulting in a judgment ordering a tenant to vacate their home within 24 hours.

On that morning in June, Cusimano ran through 11 cases in 14 minutes. Two days later, on 18 June, the morning after a tropical storm hit New Orleans, flooding parts of the city and downing trees across roadways, he heard 86 cases in 36 minutes. All but one resulted in a judgment of eviction.

Over the sessions observed by the Guardian, the tenants ordered to leave their homes included single moms, cashiers, healthcare workers and law enforcement professionals. Some had fallen behind on rent because they had been laid off from their job or missed time from work because of illness.

The majority of the cases, though, resulted in default rulings in favor of the landlord after a tenant did not appear in court. Louisiana, like nine other states, allows landlords to issue leases that waive a tenant’s right to a notice period following a missed rent payment, meaning an eviction summons can be filed almost as soon as someone falls behind. In contrast, Washington DC requires 30 days’ notice and Vermont 14 days – providing tenants more time to find legal representation, scrape together additional funds or negotiate payment plans with their landlords.

After Cusimano had issued several judgments at a hearing on 2 June, he joked with the landlords in the public benches: “No more tenants? Then we’re winning!”

The small group of renters who showed up at Cusimano’s court on the morning of 18 June included Leroyalnika Pierre, a 24-year-old single mother who works at a Waffle House and as a part-time hairstylist. She sat in the waiting area, holding her two-year-old son, waiting for Cusimano to call her name. It was her first time facing eviction and she did not know what to expect.

As she heard her name called, amid the flurry of activity, the case began before she had even made it to the judge’s bench.

“Did you pay your rent?” Cusimano asked, after the court heard from a property manager at a rental company named 1st Lake Properties, who said she owed $1,395.

“No,” she replied, her voice barely audible. “I was waiting on them to fix my place.”

Justice Cusimano immediately ordered the eviction, informing Pierre she could not withhold payment over the conditions of her apartment, but could sue 1st Lake, one of Louisiana’s largest rental firms, separately over the issue. Pierre, like almost all others that day, had no attorney. Her hearing lasted less than a minute.

“He wasn’t even trying to hear the reason why I hadn’t paid,” she said later. Her apartment was infested with termites, she claimed in a brief interview after the hearing.

During an interview, Cusimano acknowledged the speed of his hearings but said he always allowed tenants to articulate a defense.

“I don’t think I’ve ever told anyone they couldn’t be heard,” Cusimano said. “I do stop them when the stories go off on a tangent that has nothing to with the eviction, including … when they start to tell me that they were laid off. I’m not trying to be rude to them, but being laid off has nothing to do with their contract.”

He added that Louisiana law does not allow a tenant to simply stop paying rent if they have a termite infestation or other maintenance problems. If the landlord doesn’t fix things after they have been informed in writing, he noted, the renter can hire someone to make the repairs and withhold part of the rent to cover those costs.

When Louisiana’s current governor, Jeff Landry, was attorney general in 2020, his office released a document that lauded justice of the peace courts for “providing constituents with an often faster and less expensive avenue to justice”.

The volume and speed of eviction cases heard by Cusimano help explain how, in 2025, his court raised revenue of just under $1m in fees, of which Cusimano directly retained $380,929, records show. That amounted to over $63,000 more than the US chief justice, John Roberts, earned in salary last year. Cusimano has earned more money in fees alone than the nation’s chief justice in six of the last 10 years. He is also paid an additional $21,600 in parish salary, taking his earnings to more than $400,000 in 2025.

“I made a very good living last year,” Cusimano, whose court’s jurisdiction spans just over 25 sq miles, acknowledged in a recent interview.

“I am not embarrassed for the work I do,” he said. “And I think that I do the exact same work as every other justice of the peace in this state for each case. I happen to have more.

“It’s my location. It’s the numbers,” he explained. “… I have a lot of apartments in this district.”

Cusimano’s court charges at least $150 for filing an eviction – the maximum allowed by statute for justice of the peace courts that employ a clerk. Like other justices of the peace, he is entitled to keep roughly half of that amount. In some cases the court also charges an additional $60 fee for a writ of ejection, a separate order allowing the court’s constable to physically evict a tenant and their belongings from premises. A justice and their constable – an elected official who enforces the court’s decisions and also keeps a portion of filing fees – are entitled to an even split of the ejection fee.

Because justice of the peace courts are not courts of record, there is no digital record of case dockets or proceedings, making the sheer volume of eviction cases, their outcomes and who brings them almost impossible to track.

To do so, the Guardian spent three weeks inside his courtroom, and manually scanned more than 11,000 pages of eviction records from June 2025 to May 2026, to understand how these cases are handled. The records were kept individually stapled inside stacked document boxes at the side of the justice’s bench.

Data analysis by the Guardian revealed that Cusimano’s district had an eviction filing rate of almost one in five renter households per year, which would rank third out of the states and cities tracked by Princeton’s eviction lab. In the 12-month period ending this May, Cusimano’s court ruled on nearly 3,300 eviction cases. Some were handled by his son and daughter, who occasionally serve as “ad hoc” justices, records show.

The analysis also found that eviction fees were responsible for the majority of Cusimano’s salary and that 98% of the eviction filings in his court were for non-payment of rent.

Landlords pay to file an eviction and a justice issues an order, summoning the tenants to court. Each order lists the plaintiffs, the defendants and the date. Many had handwritten notes about the outcome. Filing fees are frequently billed back to tenants.

The Guardian found more than 5,500 eviction cases over a 12-month period. The fifth justice court in Jefferson, with about 30,000 renter households, has one of the highest eviction filing rates in the United States.

The Guardian found nearly 3,300 eviction judgments. A judgment can be set aside if a landlord accepts late payment but it stays on the tenant’s record.

Not every eviction filing ends in a judgment. More than 2,000 were canceled, usually because the tenant paid their late rent and any additional fees. These cases were not heard in court but the court was still paid filing fees and the tenant avoided eviction.

We could not determine the outcomes in 71 cases, either because the documents had no information or the handwriting was illegible.

A very small number of tenants won their case in court. 88 eviction orders were denied because the landlord failed to show up in court …

… and only 53 cases – less than 1% of the total eviction filings– ended in the tenant winning the case for other reasons. The records indicated only 26 tenants had a lawyer.

The data showed that one landlord – 1st Lake Properties – was responsible for over 60% of Justice Cusimano’s entire eviction docket. 1st Lake won 1,974 eviction judgments in Cusimano’s court from June 2025 to May 2026. Nineteen eviction orders were denied because 1st Lake representatives failed to show in court. Just three evictions filed by 1st Lake were denied for other reasons.

The company, which has “developed, acquired and managed” more than 10,000 rental units in Louisiana, also charges its tenants “any and all fees, including attorneys fees, and costs associated with eviction”, according to a review of 1st Lake leases and interviews with attorneys who have represented their tenants in court.

Foster, the former US justice department official, said the Guardian’s findings indicated the court was functioning as “an eviction mill and a ‘company court’”.

“When a single landlord accounts for the majority of cases in the court, when virtually all of the cases result in judgments for the landlord, when the tenants are paying for the cost of their own evictions, there is something fundamentally wrong,” said Foster, who is a co-founder of the Fines and Fees Justice Center, a non-profit group that fights against what it sees as unfair fees and fines.

During an interview, Cusimano forcefully denied that landlords repeatedly paying fees to file eviction cases in his court might represent a built-in conflict of interest.

“I don’t see a conflict at all,” he said. “It’s fee based, and they pay upfront to us, irrespective of the outcome.”

Asked about any appearance of a conflict of interest, Cusimano responded: “I don’t know. I can’t do anything about appearance.”

1st Lake was co-founded by Henry Shane Jr, a local businessman and Republican party donor. According to a 2015 media profile, Shane had used his fortune to collect more than 160 vintage cars and personally commission a recreation of the Nottoway mansion, one of the largest plantation homes built during the era of slavery.

The Guardian’s analysis of a year of Justice Cusimano’s eviction records found that 1st Lake filed an eviction claim against one out of every 10 renter households in the district, nearly all of which were for unpaid rent.

Cusimano’s court has consistently yielded the highest revenue from fees among Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts, according to a Guardian analysis of more than 3,400 annual financial filings, which are mostly handwritten and document the self-reported earnings of each justice of the peace over the past decade. The analysis revealed that the 10 justice of the peace courts in the state with the highest revenue brought in nearly $31m in fees over the past 10 years.

It also revealed that the justices in those 10 courts earned nearly $12m from their court fees over that decade and received an additional $1.2m in salaries paid by their parishes. The rest of the fees were used to compensate their constables and other staff as well as pay for office expenses and training.

Hannah Adams, a senior attorney at the National Housing Law Project, said the findings highlighted the “massive amount of money that is flowing through the system”. The non-profit, alongside the Southern Poverty Law Center, is pursuing a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Louisiana that claims the state’s justice of the peace system is unconstitutional.

“The fact that it is flowing directly into the pockets of independent judges, combined with a lack of oversight over these courts, means it is like the wild west,” she said. “There is no other state in the country that retains a system like this.”

Justice Steven Sanders, in the fifth district of East Baton Rouge, is the state’s second-highest-paid justice. His small courtroom sits on the south-eastern outskirts of the state’s capital, surrounded by low-rise housing units and next to a moving company. He holds court on a foldout table draped in black cloth.

In 2024, his court generated more than $753,000 in fees. Roughly 90% of that came from evictions, Sanders has said.

Combined with his parish salary, the part-time justice earned more than $299,000, a salary that is almost equal to what an associate justice of the US supreme court earns. Sanders, like other justices in high-revenue courts, hires a part-time clerk funded by an additional filing fee. She was paid more than $145,000 in 2024. She is also his wife.

Sanders estimated during deposition testimony in August that his court hears 300 to 400 evictions a month.

Sanders, who has served in the same role for 30 years, is the defendant in the class-action lawsuit, which was filed last year.

“Like all justices of the peace in Louisiana, Defendant Sanders’s dependence on filing fees to pay his salary and the court’s operating expenses creates an incentive for him to maximize the number of eviction cases filed in his court by ruling in favor of landlords, who select where to file a petition for eviction,” the suit claims, adding that the charging of additional fees for ejection writs “creates an incentive for him to enter judgments of eviction against tenants”.

In September, a federal judge rejected the Louisiana attorney general’s office’s attempt to have the case thrown out of court, marking a significant victory in the case.

Sanders declined to respond to written questions from the Guardian, citing ongoing litigation.

Landlords in Louisiana typically have a choice of which type of court to file eviction cases in. The state’s district and city courts also have the authority to handle eviction claims. Judges in these two more formal court systems must hold law licenses.

Litigants in justice of the peace courts also have more limited appeal rights. If tenants want to challenge a justice of the peace’s ruling, they must seek an entirely new trial in a district court. These appeals generally must be filed within 24 hours to avoid eviction, and probably mean payment of a security bond that can equal one month’s rent. They are nearly impossible to navigate without an attorney.

Established during the era of colonization, justice of the peace courts were once a mainstay of the American legal landscape.

By the 20th century, they faced closer scrutiny. In a groundbreaking 1919 American legal text, Justice and the Poor, Reginald Heber Smith argued that justice of the peace courts had formed “unholy alliances with collection agencies” and “very generally became actually corrupt”. Thanks to lack of oversight and justices’ dependence on fees, he wrote, “JP came to mean ‘judgement for the plaintiff’”.

During the last decades of the 20th century, many states moved to abolish justice of the peace courts or limit their powers. In Mississippi, the justice court was reformed following a federal appeals court decision in 1981 that found the fee system to be unconstitutional and “a malignancy weakening the administration of justice”. Now, only seven states grant these courts judicial powers, and even fewer allow their justices of the peace to handle eviction hearings, according to a review of state laws. Louisiana is the only state where justices of the peace reap income directly from the court fees they charge.

A century after Justice and the Poor was published, concerns about the system’s vulnerability to misconduct remain.

In 2019, a justice of the peace in Jefferson parish was sentenced to three years in prison for diverting money from his court to satiate a gambling addiction. In 2020, a justice of the peace in rural Morehouse parish was removed from office over a series of allegations including overcharging eviction fees. In 2021, a justice of the peace in Ascension parish resigned after local news revealed he had heard cases outside his territorial jurisdiction, which was described as a “money grab”.

In December 2025, Justice Tracy Batieste, the East Baton Rouge justice who evicted Marchana Watts, resigned from office after being temporarily disqualified by the state’s supreme court subsequent to the judiciary commission finding “substantial, credible evidence” establishing probable cause that she was charging unlawful and excessive court fees during eviction proceedings.

Batieste’s court raised more than $120,000 in revenue in 2024, according to her latest self-declared financial disclosure, ranking 10th in fees gathered by the state’s justice of the peace courts.

Recently unsealed evidence reviewed by the Guardian revealed that the justice faced sustained complaints from landlords who came before her court. One told the judiciary commission that there seemed to be “an incredible increase in fees over the past few months”.

Another indicated to the commission that Batieste’s preferred method of receiving payment was via the mobile payment service Cash App. A photograph obtained by the Guardian shows a large printout of the Cash App account pinned to a noticeboard in her courtroom.

Batieste acknowledged some of these unlawful charges, which included a “Covid fee” and additional service fees and copying fees, in unsealed sworn testimony. She also acknowledged owing her constable thousands of dollars in fees.

In March, her son Kyion, a seven-year-old with dimples and a deep smile, was killed in a car crash.

Four months later, Jackson, 27, found herself before the justice of the peace Mark Miley in East Baton Rouge, facing an eviction summons from her landlord. Jackson, who had no attorney, explained to Miley, who holds court in the boardroom of his private law office, that she had been unable to return to her job as a cashier at a local Wendy’s due to overwhelming grief.

“I attempted to go back. I just couldn’t,” she told the court. “It’s all just falling apart.”

Kyion’s funeral had cost $12,000, she later told the Guardian. Along with her overdue rent, Jackson said, she was now being charged $360 in late fees and court costs. The company was not responding to messages or maintenance requests, she said, meaning she was living without air conditioning. She had to send her infant daughter to live with relatives due to the sweltering heat.

Miley has held office since 2009. In 2025, his court, which hears eviction cases only once a week, generated $524,726 in fees, of which he retained $296,215 in compensation. At multiple instances during the Guardian’s visit he referred to the “big business” of justice of the peace courts around the parish. On a separate visit later in July, Miley offered a photographer for the Guardian a payment of two folded $20 bills alongside a small note that contained his phone number, telling them that they could spend it on “coffee”. He expressed surprise when they said they could not accept the payment.

In February of this year, Miley signed a deferred discipline agreement with the state judiciary commission after admitting that he had “regularly and knowingly” ruled over eviction cases that fell outside the geographical boundaries of his jurisdiction.

The agreement acknowledged that Miley’s conduct “gave the appearance that he was improperly presiding over the matters due to the direct financial benefit he received from the filing fees” and bound him to stop the practice.

Benton, the former legal aid attorney, said he defended about 100 eviction cases in Miley’s court between 2022 and 2024. He estimated that all but three had been improperly filed.

Less than a month after Miley signed his reprimand, the state legislature took action.

A Republican lawmaker introduced a bill to expand the borders of Miley’s district along with other justices in East Baton Rouge, across the entire territory of city court. It had the wholesale support of local landlords.

“Essentially, the way my court operates is if you file an eviction by Friday, we have court the following Thursday,” Miley told lawmakers during a legislative hearing, describing the value of expanding the boundaries of his power. “You can pull up to my office and you can get in and get out. It’s easy to access. It’s good for tenants and good for landlords, in my opinion.”

The bill was quietly passed by the state legislature – with no media coverage – and became law in June.

It had been in effect for nine days by the time Jackson appeared in Miley’s court. He listened as she told her story. She had just been able to return to work, and had taken on two jobs: one at an Amazon delivery warehouse and another for an events security company. But still, she was behind on rent.

Miley granted her an extra couple of days to find the funds, but issued a judgment of eviction nonetheless. He counseled her to contact a charity to look for financial support, and suggested his judgment against her might actually help.

“Sometimes, I’ve heard if you let a charity know you’ve got a judgment against you, it helps expedite” them offering funds, he told Jackson as he handed her a copy of the ruling against her. She appreciated the suggestion, Jackson said after the hearing.

The eviction judgment, later reviewed by the Guardian, revealed that despite the judiciary commission’s reprimand and the new law expanding his jurisdiction, Miley had still unlawfully evicted Jackson. Her rental unit was located outside his newly enlarged legal domain.

“Unlike in other states where these judges would have to remit all of their filing fees, and then be paid by fixed salary, either set by the county or the state, these justices have a literal financial incentive to break the rules,” said Adams, the National Housing Law Project attorney. “The more cases they take, if they stretch the boundaries of their jurisdiction just a few blocks further, they’re going to make more money.”

Justice Mark Spears of Jefferson parish’s second justice of the peace court holds his eviction hearings in a small office suite next to a noisy highway in the New Orleans suburb of Marrero. A crinkled US flag is tacked to the wall behind his desk.

In May this year he appeared at a rare public hearing in front of the state judiciary commission, accused of engaging in “willful misconduct” by lending “the prestige of your judicial office to advance your private interest”. Specifically, the commission admonished him for using an Instagram account named “judge.markspears” to promote himself not only as a justice but also as a private practice attorney and an NFL sports agent.

He apologized multiple times during the hearing. He acknowledged to the commissioners that he now understood that “I can’t put out to the public that I’m a justice of the peace and that I have private stuff, that I’m an attorney also. Because people would think of the prestigiousness of a judge and maybe, you know, use me as an attorney.”

Two weeks later, before an eviction docket hearing on 4 June, the court’s constable, Kendall Bussey, touted Spears’s work as a private attorney and a justice in a speech to landlords and tenants waiting for their eviction cases to be heard.

“Judge Spears is very good at what he does. He’s not only a judge, he’s also a lawyer,” Bussey said during a mass swearing-in, which took place in a cramped corridor out of the justice’s earshot. “Part of what he do is tenant-eviction law. He understands the law.”

Bussey acknowledged that tenants have a right to appeal the judge’s decisions, but added: “I will be open and honest, if Judge Spears gives you an order, 99.9% it’s not going to be overturned.” He then claimed that due to Spears’ sexpertise “the higher judges actually call him for advice when it comes to Louisiana tenant law”.

In response to questions from the Guardian, Spears distanced himself from Bussey’s remarks. “Constable Bussey is an independently elected constitutional officer. He is not my employee, I do not supervise him, and he does not speak for me or for this court.” The justice said he had never instructed Bussey or anyone else to make those kinds of statements.

“I do not hold myself out as a housing attorney,” he said. “In 20 years of practicing law, I have handled two eviction matters, and I handled both pro bono.” He added that he had never received calls from “higher judges” for advice on housing law and that he always informed litigants of their right to seek a new trial in parish court.

Spears, a former parish councilman, was first elected justice of the peace in 2019 and is running unopposed this November. His court – which is located on the West Bank of the Mississippi River across from New Orleans – has brought in more than $600,000 in fee revenue since 2020, according to his financial statements.

A 2022 recording obtained by the Guardian documents a clerk in Spears’s court explaining to an attorney why it would not be possible to waive court fees for a low-income tenant: “We are a for-profit court and we have to collect those fees.”

Spears said he “will not respond to a characterization of a four-year-old conversation to which I was not a party”.

“My court is not a ‘for-profit court’,” he said. “… If a clerk used the phrase you attribute, that was that clerk’s phrasing, not the policy of this court, and I repudiate it.”

Louisiana’s supreme court is currently considering the judiciary commission’s recommendation that Spears be suspended for six months without pay, with all but 30 days suspended. Its recommendation of discipline stated his actions had “harmed the public’s confidence in and respect for the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary”.

She lost her job about a year ago and started taking antidepressants. She developed diabetes and Cushing’s disease, she said, a hormonal condition which can be triggered by stress.

She found shelter at a relative’s home but was sleeping with four of her sons in a single bedroom. Her eldest was forced to move out.

The cost of a storage unit became unmanageable and so she sold almost all her possessions.

“Everything is still about my children,” she said. “I didn’t want them to see me go through it. That was the hardest part for me.” Over the summer she launched a GoFundMe drive to help pay for school supplies for her sons. To date, it has received no funds.

At the Jefferson parish fifth justice of the peace court one recent morning, Justice Cusimano showed journalists from the Guardian a small wad of cash, held together by a clip, that he kept inside the back of a drawer in his private office. It was about $120, he later said, adding it was held in reserve for especially “sad” eviction cases where he might offer to personally help.

In August, as the Guardian was reporting this story, Justice Cusimano announced his retirement at the end of this year, leaving the bench as perhaps the highest-paid judge in the nation.

The position will be filled without a competitive election because just one candidate is running to replace him. His name is Chuck Cusimano III.

Additional reporting Melissa Segura, Rachel Shur, Mariama Eversley, Sophie Sullivan

Additional data reporting Tom Richards, Cameron Armstrong, Mahesh Makani, Georges Lebreton, Izzy Kiff, Frederick O’Brien, Aliya Uteuova

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: From Iran to AI: the six key voter issues shaping the US midterm elections
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Much of Donald Trump’s unpopularity in polls stems from dissatisfaction over the economy and war on Iran

Next month’s midterm elections will test Donald Trump’s second term and determine whether Democrats regain political power in Washington. Polls show Trump’s approval ratings at their lowest across his two presidencies, pulled down by widespread economic dissatisfaction and an unpopular war against Iran. Here are the key issues shaping this year’s elections.

Despite Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge to tackle affordability issues, the economy consistently ranks as voters’ top concern. A recent Associated Press-NORC survey showed only 26% of voters approving of Trump’s handling of the economy, two percentage points below Joe Biden’s worst ratings on the issue.

Trump’s decision to go to war with the Tehran regime has exacerbated economic worries. Iran’s retaliatory decision to close the strait of Hormuz has driven up gasoline prices for US motorists.

It also represents a breach of his pledge to end the US’s supposed addiction to “forever wars”. Democrats and some Republicans also complain that he embarked on military action without congressional authorization.

Enforcement and closing the border remains a signature issue for Trump. He repeatedly boasts of the impact of his closure of the southern border as one of his biggest achievements, making comparisons with the performance of Joe Biden.

But the mood has since shifted. High profile violent incidents involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection agents have fed a perception that the immigration crackdown has “gone too far”.

The president is not on the ballot, but has told voters to pretend that he is. His visibility makes his character and exercise of power a central issue at a time of career-low approval ratings and a swirl of controversies over corruption allegations and his various pet building projects.

Democrats have framed the midterms as an opportunity to rein in the president.

AI has emerged as a key campaign issue, with surveys showing a majority of voters holding negative views on it, even as Trump champions its development and attempts to rename it “super intelligence”.

Up to 70% of Americans oppose the construction of AI datacenters in their areas, polls show.

The elections will take place against a backdrop of uncertainty over whether Trump will try to interfere with the vote. The US supreme court last month rejected his bid to restrict mail-in ballots, triggering an intensification of unfounded accusations from him about election fraud.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Why are French police so violent? Their job is to protect the state, not the people
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Officers are instruments of state whose job is to repress, rather than manage, public dissent

Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.

While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.

The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.

French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.

Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.

French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.

That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and their continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.

Defence ball launchers, for example, fire rubber projectiles at 185mph (300kph). The explosive grenades that injured gilets jaunes protesters in the late 2010s and killed an environmental protester in 2014 have been phased out, but been replaced by pyrotechnic stun grenades.

Designed to disperse crowds through both impact and a 160dB acoustic shock, these have caused multiple injuries in recent years, including lost eyes and teeth, fractured jaws and several amputated limbs. They also frequently instil mass panic.

Violent policing methods are also fostered by France’s almost unique culture of street protest. A legacy of insurrection dating back to the 1789 revolution means protesters know the street can, and generally does, force governments to back down.

Unlike in Germany or the Netherlands, French unions, while they may strike often, are not formal government negotiating partners. The top-heavy, presidential structure of the Fifth Republic marginalises institutional consultation.

That means a heavily centralised state often passes laws with little popular agreement, making the “power of the street” one of citizens’ few viable means of forcing concessions. Protest here is regarded as a civic duty and a legitimate democratic tool.

That creates a vicious circle. French authorities see large crowds as an existential threat, so send in the police. Their military-style tactics entrench the aggression and alienate peaceful demonstrators. This prompts the more radical groups to opt for more violent tactics. But rather than isolating those elements, police respond with baton charges and munitions. And that turns protests into battles.

Data from conflict monitoring organisations, such as Acled, consistently shows that France, perhaps surprisingly, does not always record western Europe’s highest number of demonstrations (Germany and Italy also vie for that title).

But it does show that France consistently records the highest rates of escalated, high-intensity unrest, including street barricades, widespread vandalism and looting, arson attacks and direct confrontations between protesters and police.

France’s approach to policing and crowd management has for decades drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors and civil society groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Council of Europe.

Reports have documented instances of excessive force, misuse of grenades and rubber bullets, arbitrary mass arrests and routine teargas deployment against largely non-violent protesters. But the model persists, and is even expanding.

Last month, thousands marched in protest at a proposed “licence to kill” law seeking to establish a legal “presumption of self-defence” for police officers and gendarmes using firearms in the line of duty.

The law, opposed by civil rights groups, leftwing politicians, the magistrates’ union and the UN, would in effect shift the burden of proof on to victims and their families to demonstrate that a police shooting was disproportionate.

In essence, critics argue, it would institutionalise police impunity; reinforcing, once more, a security culture that treats public dissent and social tension not as democratic realities to be managed, but as insurrections to be repressed. The battle for France’s streets is far from over.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.text:
These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?

Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.

For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.

Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).

Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.

No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?

Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.

The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.

Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).

And so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …

Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and the tricolore of Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. He made the news in June when hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.

To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”

Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”

In a 2024 study, Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.

Oxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.

Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones use more than 500 litres of diesel per hour, releasing CO2 as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about 16m tonnes of CO2 annually. It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO2. In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.

And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.

Ecocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”

Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”

Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capitalist class” who operate outside and above borders and rules. Look at the stern of the superyachts, under the name, and they’re almost all registered in places such as the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, the Isle of Man and Malta – flag states offering, among other benefits, tax neutrality.

It’s hard to hide a superyacht, or ownership of one. We know about Mark Zuckerberg’s 118-metre Launchpad, and Jeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru, estimated to have cost €444m. Koru caused a stir in 2022, when a historic bridge in Rotterdam, a Dutch national monument, was going to be dismantled in order to let it through. After the uproar its masts were stepped downstream in the end. Koru is actually a sailing yacht, which might sound like a greener way of doing it, but then Bezos also has a 75-metre support vessel, with additional crew accommodation, helipad, submarine, speedboats and cars, that follows Koru around like a loyal dog. Zuckerberg’s got a couple of support vessels too.

Roman Abramovich is another big fan of a yacht. Using leaked documents, Forbes counted 16 belonging to the Russian oligarch. My ship location app tells me that the superest of his fleet – Solaris (140-metres) and Eclipse (162-metres), both registered in the Cook Islands – are now parked in the Sea of Marmara, near Istanbul. When western governments seized Russian oligarchs’ assets after the invasion of Ukraine, Turkey refused to join the sanctions and became a bolt-hole.

Eclipse doesn’t even eclipse everything. The world’s longest superyacht, at 180-metres, is Azzam, launched in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, who died in 2022, but according to Boat International and the Superyacht Fan website, Azzam is still in the family. When you get to this level it’s not always clear who owns a yacht, as they can be held in trusts or shell companies, sometimes across several jurisdictions.

Take Dilbar for example – a little shorter than Azzam but the world’s largest by volume. In June Bloomberg reported that a court in Germany had ruled that sanctions no longer applied to the yacht after finding insufficient evidence that the Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov controls The Sister Trust, which formally owns the vessel.

Or Kosatka, formerly Graceful, the 82-metre yacht seen being escorted through Danish waters by Russian naval vessels in the summer and widely reported to be linked to Vladimir Putin. A bigger, 140-metre yacht, the €620m Scheherazade, which boasts two helipads, anti-drone technology and a cryotherapy room, remains impounded in Italy. Activists working for poisoned Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny believe that one is also owned by Putin.

There is no secret about who owns the aptly named Leviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show. Co-founder and president of the video game company Valve, Gabe Newell doesn’t just own the 111-metre Leviathan, he also owns the 93-metre support vessel Draak, parked up next door.

I am allowed on to Leviathan and get a brief look around. I’m shown the huge mess area, which Newell and his guests share with the 42 crew. As well as the pool, there’s an outdoor cinema, basketball court, and a huge gaming lounge with consoles and race simulators, open to everyone. The crew are also keen to point out Leviathan’s diesel-electric hybrid propulsion and battery energy storage system. But it still has a 494,000-litre fuel tank. Fill ’er up? Certainly sir, that’ll be roughly a million euros.

It’s not total eco denial at the Monaco Yacht Show however, there’s at least some acknowledgment of environmental impact. I drop in on the Blue Wake awards, “for solutions delivering measurable impact on yachting sustainability”. So there’s a prize for a company using more sustainable materials for yacht interiors. A yacht wins a Blue Wake for having sails, and a marina gets one for planting Posidonia plants.

This is all good news … but actually, when you look at it, it’s not that good. In five years 3,000 sq metres of Posidonia have been restored – sounds impressive, but then by my calculations that’s an area of about 55 metres by 55 metres. The boat with sails? Great, but actually there are fewer sailing boats here than in previous years, the trend is towards power, more and more of it.

It looks like greenwashing, token gestures. I have an Italian friend who calls these superyachts stronzi di mare – turds of the sea. And you know what you can’t do to a turd. There’s no escaping the truth: that they drink fossil fuels like there’s no tomorrow, which there won’t be if they’re allowed to carry on; that there’s no more monstrous symbol of inequality; and that they look like irons.

But before storming off in disgust, maybe I’ll just pop into that wine tasting. In my socks.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: ‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt?

Espresso Embassy, a third-wave coffee shop in Budapest’s diplomatic and governmental quarter, is where visiting reporters and academics come to talk politics. On the way in for my morning coffee on 18 March, I passed a poster for Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party that had been vandalised with a marker pen: “the safe choice” had become “the certain way to get fucked”. From across the cafe, I spotted the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum locked in conversation, possibly with a source. I heard someone exclaim: “Just like Mussolini!” It was election season in Hungary.

It was also a couple of days before Cpac Hungary, a satellite event of the US-based conservative conference. As members of the international right arrived in town, the notorious Orbánist thinktank known as the Danube Institute was hosting an event called On Censorship, Tolerance, the Left and God. The official line would be: bad, good, bad, good.

After dark, I walked along the walls of Buda castle and past the Jesuit stairs to the institute. The featured speakers were Dave Rubin, an American podcaster from the so-called “intellectual dark web”, and Eva Vlaardingerbroek, a Dutch provocateur who claimed the title “shieldmaiden of the far right” on her X profile. “You don’t realise how good you have it” in Hungary, Rubin said. “So many things are wrong across the west.” After the panel, an American man introduced himself to me and asked how long I’d been in Budapest. Had I ever considered dual citizenship? If so, he could help. “My friends,” he said, “call me the Harriet Tubman of white people.”

For the previous few months, I’d been hanging around the Danube Institute and other state-subsidised gathering places, trying to pass as yet another member of the rightwing intelligentsia making his pilgrimage to Budapest. Founded in 2013 with state funds redirected by the Orbán government, the institute had become known as the central hub in the emerging “postliberal” movement, a loose coalition of heterodox conservative thinkers frequently associated with the idiosyncratic American blogger and self-styled Christian dissident Rod Dreher. During Dreher’s first fellowship term at the Danube Institute in 2021, he helped arrange Tucker Carlson’s weeklong press junket in Hungary, which featured a fawning Fox News interview with Orbán. Since then, liberal publications such as the New York Times, the New Yorker and the Atlantic have dispatched journalists to grill Dreher about the institute and his relationship to Orbán’s autocratic regime. This produced a series of breathless reports that showcased the small thinktank as a clearinghouse for dangerous illiberal ideas. As Applebaum wrote in her book Twilight of Democracy: “The Danube Institute exists, in practice, to make the Hungarian government presentable to the outside world.”

In Applebaum’s view, the Orbán regime had “created a political system in which no opposition party could possibly win”, and the foreign intellectuals at the Danube Institute were either cynical propagandists or naive stooges for Orbán’s anti-democratic project. But soon, Orbán would be out of power, ousted in a landslide election in April, and in June the new Hungarian parliament would pass a constitutional amendment dismantling the patronage system that funds the Danube Institute, as well as MCC Brussels, a training ground for Fidesz elites.

It was end times for the postliberals in Budapest, even if they didn’t know it yet. What will survive the demise of the so-called Budapest scene is a fractured group of rightwing thinkers who, whatever their fate in Hungary, will continue to hold a frightening level of influence over US political culture. If they were ever Orbán’s puppets, they aren’t any more. But reducing them to the unthinking servants of one particular strongman has made it more difficult to confront the real threat of postliberal ideas – or the crisis to which they are responding.

Officially, I was in Budapest to write a book about the western intellectuals who travelled to Hungary to meet the dissident opposition during the final years of the communist era. My family and I were guests of the Institute for Advanced Study, which had once been called the Collegium Budapest before it was effectively closed by the Orbán government in 2011. Now reopened, it was part of the rump of Central European University that still remained in Hungary. The rest of the institution was forced to move to Vienna during a prolonged campaign against George Soros and Hungary’s independent civil society.

At the start of this year, I made it my half-ironic mission to infiltrate the Danube Institute. I really did want to see what was actually going on inside this thinktank that had become known as the headquarters of the international postliberal project. Reaching it was not hard. It is housed in the Lónyay-Hatvany Villa, a refurbished building that had briefly served as an SS casino during the second world war and now housed a high-end restaurant on its main floor. One evening, I climbed a steep staircase dimly lit by iron sconces, the yellow light reflecting off wet stone, until I reached a narrow passage closed in by two high walls. Up ahead, I noticed a doorway marked only by a floor lamp on a small red carpet. I hesitated, then entered.

Straight in front of me was a dining room with a commanding view of the Danube. I snapped a few photos with my phone until I heard someone behind me on the stairs. I hurried into the basement annexe and reached a check-in table. I gave a young assistant my name, and she pointed towards a coat check. It turned out that infiltrating the Danube Institute just required online registration.

In the brightly lit basement, a shelf offered complimentary issues of glossy rightwing journals such as The European Conservative and Hungarian Review. I picked up a copy of the then state-subsidised Hungarian Conservative with a painting by Tivadar Csontváry Kosztka on the cover; its title was Mysterious Island.

The other guests were beginning to arrive, and I was immediately worried I’d been misled by a New Yorker piece on Dreher, in which he told a journalist that “the Danube Institute had a casual dress code” and he “could usually leave the suits at the apartment” even when meeting with ministers from Orbán’s Fidesz party. But here was a parade of male intellectual fashion: ribbed turtlenecks; crocheted ties and silk cravats; blazers of tweed, linen and corduroy. I looked down at my rumpled blazer – the only one I own – and felt underdressed.

In the months to come, I would jot down scraps of overheard conversation. Much of it was unsurprising, especially for anyone who had spent time on X: “We’re going to interrogate him with truth serum”, “No one is linking except Tucker”, “Hitler would have gone broke on her OnlyFans”, “Do you have a contact for Vance?”

All the knowing gossip and memes were part of a game of one-upmanship among intellectuals who styled themselves as insiders. Still, there was something jarring about seeing this very online culture in the flesh. Most of the names they dropped were exactly the ones you’d expect. What did catch me off guard was how often I also heard them mention the names of the liberal journalists who had alerted me to the existence of the Danube Institute in the first place. If Hungary looms large for people like Applebaum, she, in turn, haunts the postliberal imagination; these guys all clearly read the Atlantic.

“Anne Applebaum, I think she’s great,” I overheard one of the institute’s fellows wisecrack at the bar. “I really respect her.” At the very first event I attended, a debate on How Non-Liberal Regimes Rule Through the Good Life, the main speaker referred to Applebaum as “persona non grata” at the Danube Institute. The postliberal economist Philip Pilkington responded: “I do find the descent into Applebaumism hilarious.”

Pilkington was referring to Applebaum’s stubborn tendency to divide the world between liberal democracies and illiberal autocracies, between virtuous and corrupt elites. This “moral purity test” was not only hypocritical, he pointed out, it was intellectually unserious. According to Pilkington, it prevented liberal elites from accurately seeing themselves. The “crude” Applebaum analysis, he said, doesn’t “have a good explanation of why liberalism is falling apart”.

Part of the appeal of postliberalism is that it does provide an account of why it feels as though everything is falling apart: a liberal world order could never have turned out otherwise. At least this is Pilkington’s view, as expressed in his 2025 book, The Collapse of Global Liberalism. Born in Ireland, Pilkington is a millennial former leftist who took a job in finance and then moved to Hungary, where until June he was employed at the Danube Institute and the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, then another Fidesz-aligned thinktank. For him, “liberalism is, in the final analysis, a dark and uncivilised philosophy of life that will destroy any civilisation it touches”.

Equally comfortable making sweeping claims about “Marxian historical materialism” and offering hot takes about yoga pants as a symptom of civilisational decline, Pilkington argues that the drive to demolish all hierarchies is “self-undermining” and “self-destructive”: “The reality is that equality does not exist in most spheres.” Liberal capitalism, according to this line of thought, only ever appeared stable because it was built on a foundation of pre-liberal hierarchical structures, such as the church, family and classical legal traditions. Now it has become a victim of its own self-undermining success. As Pilkington puts it, “liberal capitalism” became “far too aggressive in its promotion of work and consumption and is undermining the building blocks on which the stability of society rests”, namely “the family and the ability to reproduce the species”.

The postliberal movement’s foundational text is 2018’s Why Liberalism Failed by the philosopher Patrick Deneen, another visitor to the Danube Institute. The title of Deneen’s book captures the shared premise of all postliberal thought: that the historical period in which western societies were governed by a “regime of liberalism”, as he put it elsewhere, has already reached a calamitous end. Whether that period began in 1989 with the fall of communist regimes in central and eastern Europe or 500 years ago with the Protestant reformation remains a matter of some obfuscation.
