For postliberals, the collapse of liberalism was an inevitable outgrowth of its first principles: its anti-hierarchical commitment to formal equality, its faith in human progress and, above all, its emphasis on individual autonomy. In practice, Deneen argues, these values actually produced extreme economic inequality, spiritual debasement and a profound sense of unfreedom. “Liberalism has failed,” he writes, “not because it fell short, but because it was true to itself.”

At least initially, the postliberals seemed more solicitous of the populist masses than of the Republican old guard: they supported Donald Trump, who was then styling himself as a champion for a new working-class coalition against the elite establishment. Deneen and other postliberals claimed their goal was to transcend the toxic left-right divide in US politics by positioning themselves as both allies of social democracy and enemies of corporate progressivism. Indeed, they insisted the only way to defeat the disastrous post-cold war alliance between neoliberal economics and neoconservative foreign policy was through a novel fusion of social-conservative values and left economic ideas.

After postliberalism relocated to Hungary it became more true to itself. The year after its publication, Why Liberalism Failed was translated into Hungarian, and Deneen met Orbán in Budapest. In the years after 2018, the Danube Institute and other regime-supported institutions hosted nearly every major American postliberal intellectual in Budapest. Many are now familiar figures on the so-called New Right. To use a basketball analogy, if Deneen was the philosopher-coach and Dreher was the veteran point guard on this postliberal squad, the rest of the starting five might include the Catholic integralist Adrian Vermeule; the national conservative Yoram Hazony; the censorious culture warrior Christopher Rufo; and the shapeshifting opinion columnist, UnHerd editor and Compact magazine cofounder Sohrab Ahmari, with the political theorist Gladden Pappin coming in off the bench.

Back in the US, Pappin had been a junior academic before he began writing blog posts for the Journal of American Greatness under the pen name Manlius Capitolinus. By now, all of Pappin’s posts as Manlius Capitolinus have been taken down, but he subsequently published a series of revealing essays under his own name in another journal. In Toward a Party of the State, from 2019, Pappin argued that the “liberal conservatism” of the old Republican establishment had failed precisely because it became a handmaid to the “governing ideology of neoliberalism”, a form of statecraft without a moral vision of the good life.

Drawing on left thinkers such as Nancy Fraser, Pappin suggested that neoliberalism maintained its fragile legitimacy by “redefining itself as progressive”, creating an unholy alliance between pro-corporate and socially liberal constituencies. To overcome the “neoliberal ideological hegemony”, according to this theory, we need a national unity government with a strong, activist party-state led by intellectuals, among them, presumably, Pappin himself.

At the time, postliberals could still squint and see Trump as a vessel for this project. After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Pappin visited Budapest for the first time, and before long, he had relocated to Hungary. In 2023, he was appointed president of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, a highly unusual position for a foreign national. Pappin now had the opportunity to learn from the Fidesz party-state and start putting his ideas into practice.

To postliberals, Orbán’s governing programme looked like a dream come true. As Rufo, coming off his stint at the Danube Institute, put it in 2023: “Hungary’s leaders are serious people combating the same forces confronted by conservatives in the west: the fraying of national culture, entrenched leftwing institutions and the rejection of sexual difference.” But, compared with the contemporary Republican party, Orbán seemed exhilaratingly willing to use the power of the state to pursue a conservative vision of the good life.

Orbán was the great defender of the postliberal trinity: “strong families, strong borders, strong industry,” as Pappin said in an interview with the Atlantic. “Orbánomics” consisted of a series of interventions to build up Hungary’s car manufacturing capacity, ensure access to less expensive Russian energy and increase work requirements for welfare recipients, raising taxes on banks and even nationalising some.

Defying the EU, the Orbán regime also pursued a so-called “zero migration” policy. But the postliberals were perhaps most enamoured of Orbán’s efforts to encourage traditional family formation and raise the birthrate. Since 2022, Hungary has spent about 5% of its GDP every year on a suite of welfare initiatives offering generous maternity leave, childcare support and tax breaks for mothers.

As Rufo explained, these seemingly “progressive” policies were meant to serve “conservative ends”: first, “to incentivise traditional marriage and family formation”; second, to help ward off “foreign ideologies, such as critical race theory and gender ideology”; and, third, because “raising the native Hungarian birthrate obviates the need for foreign immigration”. Hungary’s student debt policy also allowed new mothers to suspend, reduce or ultimately erase their debt entirely, depending on how many children they had given birth to. In 2023, Pappin pointed to Hungary’s student debt programme as a model for the kinds of policies the Republican party should pursue.

During the Biden years, the postliberals yearned for the kind of power and stability in the US that Orbán enjoyed in Hungary. In Deneen’s 2023 book Regime Change: Toward a Postliberal Future, the philosopher was no longer just diagnosing the problem with liberalism; he was suggesting a radical solution. Deneen now called for a revolutionary turn to “aristopopulism”, in which a cadre of elites would act as “class traitors” to help socially conservative workers depose the liberal-meritocratic ruling class in the US, and take control of a newly integrated state and civil society. “What is needed, in short,” he wrote, “is … the peaceful but vigorous overthrow of a corrupt and corrupting liberal ruling class and the creation of a postliberal order in which existing political forms can remain in place, as long as a fundamentally different ethos informs those institutions and the personnel who populate key offices and positions.” As an example of what he had in mind, Deneen pointed to Hungary.

By the time I arrived in Budapest in late 2025, Trump was back in power, with the postliberal darling JD Vance as his vice-president. The new administration was armed with a blueprint for Deneen-style regime change. In 2023, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative US thinktank, had released a report titled Project 2025, “75% of which is being implemented”, as Heritage’s’s Paul McCarthy, who’d been involved in drafting the chapter on US foreign aid, claimed at a Danube Institute event this February. (The Danube Institute and Heritage had established a formal collaboration in March 2023, a month before the Project 2025 report was released.)

For Applebaum and other post-cold war liberal intellectuals such as the historian Timothy Snyder, the direction of the US right was yet more evidence that “America’s future is Hungary”. According to Snyder, Trump and Vance are “Orbán’s pupils”, and many of their policy decisions “arise in whole or in part from Hungarian sources”.

But in Hungary, a funny thing was happening: Orbán’s own government was no longer popular. Péter Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who had broken with the party, was leading Orbán by double digits in independent polls. One of two things was about to happen: either Fidesz would be out of power for the first time in 16 years, or Orbán would prove himself a genuine dictator. The Applebaum theory of Orbán’s regime was about to be put to the test, and so was postliberalism.

On the national holiday of 15 March, I joined masses of supporters of Magyar’s new Tisza party as they filled the streets all the way up to Heroes’ Square, where Orbán had made his first major political speech in June 1989. Later that year, Orbán raced back to Budapest from his Soros-funded scholarship at Oxford to participate in the unfolding regime change as a representative of Fidesz, founded as the Federation of Young Democrats. Now, my Hungarian friends were joking that Orbán resembled one of the corpulent bureaucrats he had once sought to replace.

In the Hungary of 2026, postliberalism was not working out as planned. Inflation and house prices had risen faster than anywhere else in the EU. Orbánomics was crashing out. Industrial development hadn’t resulted in the promised economic growth, and Fidesz had been rocked by a massive pollution scandal at an electric vehicle battery plant. Though migration was effectively halted, Chinese guest workers streamed in to work in the newly created car industry jobs. After creeping up marginally, the fertility rate seemed to be flattening.

Corruption throughout Orbán’s patronage system was so rampant that Hungary was being widely labeled a mafia state. Fidesz had rewritten the constitution, installed party loyalists in key judicial roles, gerrymandered electoral districts, changed election laws to inflate their parliamentary majority, put much of the higher education sector under the control of boards stacked with party members and overseen the sale of media companies to regime-friendly oligarchs. Already, the regime had granted that women with at least four children did not have to pay income taxes for the rest of their lives. In the run-up to the election, they reduced the number of children required to three, and then two. But that wasn’t going to be enough to win an election, let alone replace the global neoliberal economic order.

Both Trump and Vance had been rumoured guests at Cpac Hungary, but neither showed up in the end. The event chair still claimed that the “biggest stars of the sovereigntist right” were all on the way to Budapest. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, was a last-minute addition. They also advertised an appearance by the Czech prime pinister, populist billionaire Andrej Babiš, but he pulled out at the last minute. Maybe they had all been scared off by Orbán’s tanking poll numbers.

Lingering outside the gate on the day of the event itself, I saw Pappin walking toward the VIP entrance. I ducked behind a Cpac banner reading “FEL GYŐZELEMRE!” (“ON TO VICTORY!”).

I wondered how he was taking the polls. A little over a week earlier, I had run into Pappin after an event at which he had joked that the liberal Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, sounded a lot like a “dangerous postliberal” when he prominently declared that the crisis in the rules-based international order was “a rupture, not a transition”. I was grabbing a coffee at a Scruton cafe – part of a chain named after the conservative English philosopher and Orbán ally Roger Scruton. Exposed lightbulbs hung from the ceiling in front of a stencilled cartoon of a hip, young Scruton in a double-breasted suit, with a speech bubble: “The greatest treasure of Hungarians is their national identity.” When I spotted Pappin at the next table, I decided to introduce myself, playing up the extent to which Scruton himself figures into my research. We talked about life in Budapest, the city he had referred to elsewhere as “Scrutopia”, and he scoffed at the impression of the Danube milieu put forward by the western press. “You know, all these people show up in Budapest looking for some kind of conservative intellectual utopia,” he said. Though the scene had been influential, he added, “There are only like five of us.”

Five intellectuals in close proximity to power can do a lot of damage. Take it from Deneen in Regime Change: “Even if relatively small, an elite cadre skilled at directing and elevating popular resentments, combined with the political power of the many, can bolster populist political prospects as a working governmental and institutional force.” But this wasn’t what was happening in Hungary, at least not any more. The political power of the many was no longer cooperating. Though Vance had finally flown in for support, the polls still weren’t moving in Orbán’s direction.

On 11 April, the night before the election, I heard Orbán’s voice echoing from the castle during a final torch-lit rally. The next day, the city was all nerves. The final turnout, nearly 80%, would set a national record. After polls closed, I gathered with friends to stream the independent Partizán media feed on YouTube. The first results, released just after 8pm, put Fidesz slightly ahead. Then, at 9.16pm, a new banner crossed the bottom of the screen: Orbán had called Magyar to concede. The convoluted Hungarian election machine had backfired, and Tisza had defeated Fidesz in a landslide. “Looks like the last bastion is gone,” Eva Vlaardingerbroek posted on X.

My friends and I rushed to Batthyány Square, where Magyar was set to give his victory speech. The crowd throbbed with expectation; drones circled above us. Techno music drifted across the Danube from a dance party next to the floodlit parliament. We eavesdropped on two childhood friends who hadn’t seen each other in years as they embraced and looked deeply into one another’s eyes in wonder. Their meet-cute was interrupted by someone vomiting on the cobblestone at their feet.

It slowly dawned on me that what we were witnessing was not a change of government but a regime change. Throughout the campaign, Magyar had used the Hungarian term rendszerváltás, literally “system change”, once reserved for talking about the democratic transition from communism in 1989, and now, somehow, Tisza had made it happen.

If Pilkington is right that post-cold war liberals don’t have a good understanding of why their world is falling apart, neither did the postliberals after Magyar’s win. For them, the fact that Orbán had conceded gracefully was proof that he had always been committed to democracy – and that liberal critics such as Applebaum and Snyder had misunderstood him all along. On election night, Rod Dreher responded to news that Orbán had conceded with a sarcastic post on X: “But … but … but, I was told by so many experts and journalists in the west that this would never happen, that Orbán is a fascist dictator who would never surrender power!”

It’s true that Applebaum’s work often relied on a reductive binary between democracy and autocracy that, in this case, had obscured the fact that democratic change was still very much possible in Hungary. But the postliberals were trapped in their own binaries, too: because Orbán wasn’t a dictator, their logic went, Hungary must have ultimately been a democracy. This allowed them to dismiss all the ways Fidesz had held on to power by changing election laws, packing the judiciary, attacking civil society and higher education, and consolidating control over the media.

There was one thing that Applebaum and the postliberals could agree on after the election: the demise of the so-called Hungarian model. Applebaum’s post-election column marked the passing of one of her own stock narratives. Orbán’s Hungary would no longer serve, she wrote, “as a model for Americans or Europeans who want to capture their own states, or take apart their own checks and balances, or impose their own illiberal ideologies on people who don’t accept them”. In his own postmortem, Dreher reached a similar conclusion: “As a model for Maga and other nationalist conservatives in the west, Hungary is over.” But it would be a mistake to think that Orbán’s defeat, or the potential closure of state-supported institutions such as the Danube Institute, means the end of postliberalism.

“We are all postliberals now,” Pilkington argued on Postliberal Order, the Substack newsletter he shares with Deneen, Pappin and CC Pecknold, a historian of theology. As he pointed out, Magyar shared many of Orbán’s views on core issues. “From the standpoint of domestic politics, Magyar effectively ran on Fidesz’s own platform,” Pilkington argued in a different post-election column, “promising to keep migration low, maintain Hungarian cultural nationalism, and keep the generous family support system that Fidesz built in place.” But Pilkington wasn’t just making a narrow political point. Postliberalism as an intellectual project was not tied to the fate of any particular political party. “No doubt, Fidesz has been an incubator of alternative thinking in transatlantic conservatism, but these ideas are in the ether and are unlikely to go away any time soon.”

In the narrow, descriptive sense, it’s true that there is no going back to the liberalism of the brief, post-cold war interregnum, circa 1989-2015. Still, postliberals are terrible at predicting what comes next. On X, Pilkington posts regular prophecies of western civilisational catastrophe with the swagger of a former finance guy. “There is an old phrase in investment,” he writes in The Collapse of Global Liberalism, “it is better to be wrong for the right reasons than right for the wrong reasons.”

But if Pilkington is right about our new postliberal era, it is for the wrong reasons. Clearly, the world of post-cold war liberalism is over. But the idea that all the challenges brought on by its collapse can be answered by the postliberal programme is a farce. As Hungary has shown, postliberal policies don’t produce a life good enough to win over voters. In the end, Hungary was a false model for our authoritarian future. Now the model we have to worry about is US-made.

In all my time in Hungary, there was one person I had never seen at the Danube Institute or at any of the other events I attended: Rod Dreher, an alleged mainstay of the Budapest scene. After a few failed attempts, we finally met on a spring afternoon in early May, the day before Magyar was sworn in as prime minister. Over rosé spritzes and nicotine pouches, I made my confession to Dreher: I told him I had been attending events at the Danube Institute, about all the wild conversations I had overheard, and about how I was just trying to understand what attracted American intellectuals to the dissident right. We both agreed that Hungary was a strange place to look for lessons about the US. But here we both were.

“I was never part of any scene here, although I kind of thought I would be,” he told me. Like Pappin, he noted that only a handful of conservative anglophone intellectuals lived in Budapest; most of their companions were only there temporarily, to check out what it was like when their side was in power. But the Scruton cafes were “phoney”, more Ikea than English country house. The Danube Institute, though it was never the Orbánist propaganda factory it was rumoured to be, was overseen by overcautious Hungarian managers, he said, who had held it back from becoming a truly stimulating intellectual environment. “There was a scene,” he admitted, “but it was very superficial.”

And now the Budapest scene, however superficial, was coming to an end. Over the next few months, the new Tisza-led parliament would pass a series of laws and constitutional amendments aimed at dismantling the Fidesz party’s system of funding thinktanks and other intellectual institutions. At the end of July, Pappin would resign from the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, and the MCC foundation would be formally dissolved. Already, Magyar had promised not only to end government funding of the organisation that runs Cpac Hungary, but to investigate the former funding through the newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. As Dreher would later put it: “The unsettling atmosphere of vengeance that has overtaken Hungary since Péter Magyar became prime minister [sic] likely means the end of the Danube Institute.” (The Danube Institute did not respond to requests for comment.)

I asked Dreher what he would do next. He told me he had briefly considered moving to Vienna, but then he had had a change of heart. It was time to give up the good life in central Europe and return to the American south. My own temporary resident permit was about to expire. As the sun set behind Károlyi-kert, one of the oldest gardens in Budapest, Dreher and I downed our last rosé spritzes. Postliberalism was finally coming home, and so were we.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Man who heckled El-Sayed is son of Republican adviser who was paid for ‘influencer marketing’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Timmy Teepell’s firm paid $250,000 by America Next, which has been trying to gin up ‘organic’ opposition to El-Sayed

The man who attempted to ambush the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed with a question about his supposed allegiance to the Muslim Brotherhood – which El-Sayed parlayed into a viral clip for his campaign – is the son of a political operator who recently received $250,000 for “canvassing and influencer marketing” against El-Sayed, the Guardian has learned.

In the now-famous exchange, a man – first identified by the Handbasket as Thomas “Tommy” Teepell – asked El-Sayed if he would “disavow” the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed said he would, but then asked: “What are you implying? Do you assume that I wouldn’t?” What followed was a five-minute exchange that has drawn over 50m views across several social media platforms, in which El-Sayed queries the man about the guarantees of religious freedom in the constitution.

Teepell is the son of Timothy “Timmy” Teepell, a longtime strategist for the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley as well as former Republican Louisiana governor Bobby Jindal. Timmy Teepell’s firm, Breakthrough LLC, was paid $250,000 on 29 September by America Next, a 501(c)(4) non-profit with which it shares a Baton Rouge office suite, according to a filing with the Federal Election Commission (FEC).

The filing says the money would fund the canvassing and influencer marketing in opposition to El-Sayed. It is the only independent expenditure the group has reported since 2015, when it paid OnMessage Inc for television advertising backing Bobby Jindal’s presidential campaign.

America Next has been trying to gin up “organic” town hall opposition to El-Sayed, as the Handbasket report noted. On 1 October, a member of the University of Michigan College Republicans, saying he was acting for America Next, reportedly offered students $200 to boo and question El-Sayed at a town hall in Flint.

The same Baton Rouge suite is also the registered address of a Christian non-profit for which Teepell is the registered agent, and whose four directors include two other Teepell family members. Hawley’s campaign committee has also paid Breakthrough. (The Handbasket report also outlines the close relationship between Sean Feucht and the elder Teepell.)

Pennsylvania business records list Timmy Teepell as a director of Sean Feucht’s ministry, which owns a townhouse on Capitol Hill in Washington.

Timmy Teepell, Thomas Teepell, America Next and Hawley’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nothing in the filings shows that Thomas Teepell was paid by Breakthrough or America Next.

Jindal launched America Next as a policy non-profit in 2013, and its website still publishes his columns. The group does not disclose its donors. In the year to July 2024 its tax filings reported $5,066,000 in contributions.

Other groups’ tax filings show where some of the money came from. American Action Network, a group the Guardian has previously described as a dark-money outfit and which is connected to House Republican leaders, gave America Next $500,000 for “issue support” in its tax year ending in June 2022, according to its tax filing for that year. Secure Florida’s Future, a 501(c)(4) based in Tallahassee, gave America Next $250,000 in 2022, according to its own filing.

In 2022, America Next paid OnMessage Inc $5,020,808 for “media services and consulting”, against total expenses of $10,130,638, according to its 990 filing for the year.

America Next has also funded Republican Super Pacs, giving them at least $1,475,000 since 2018, FEC records show.

The ministry’s tax filings do not show when he joined either. Its most recent public return, for 2020, lists three directors: John Feucht, Robert Zoellner and Alvin Chun. It does not mention Timmy Teepell or OnMessage, as RNS reported in 2024. The ministry’s revenue that year was $5,314,148, up from $283,526 in 2019. IRS records now classify Sean Feucht Ministries as a church, a category that is not required to file public returns, and list no return after 2020.

In June 2025, former staffers accused Feucht of “potential financial crimes” and spiritual abuse, and said that “the members of Mr Feucht’s board have potentially failed in their fiduciary duty to exercise appropriate oversight”, as RNS reported.

In a video posted on 11 June 2025, Feucht said “none of those allegations are true”, describing his accusers as “embittered, angry, upset … former volunteers” who “know nothing about our financial situation”. He said: “Every single penny that has been raised that you guys out there have donated has gone to fulfill its kingdom-ordained purpose.”

Separately, a California donor is suing Sean Feucht Ministries in federal court for fraud. The complaint, filed in March, alleges that a $250,000 donation solicited in 2023 for Feucht’s Let Us Worship tour was “diverted, in whole or in part, to other uses controlled by Mr Feucht”. A judge dismissed the original complaint in September, finding that the fraud claims had not been pleaded with enough specificity, but allowed the donor to amend it, and an amended complaint was filed on 30 September. The ministry has argued that the claims are time-barred and barred by the church autonomy doctrine.

Their website testimony named Zoellner as a board member of Sean Feucht Ministries, and alleged that former key employees “were never made aware of their names”. It did not name Timmy Teepell. Feucht did not respond to RNS’s request for comment at the time.

Feucht has prayed in public for the elder Teepell’s political work. Laying hands on Teepell at an event in Florida, Feucht said, “We pray that Timmy would put more revivalists in public office,” according to RNS. A video shows Feucht praying over Teepell and his family. Teepell was also on the bill at Feucht’s “Hold the Line” conference at the Trump International hotel in Washington on 11 September 2021, scheduled to speak on “2022 Forecast and Polling”, according to the event’s listing on Eventbrite, which gives his name as “Timmy Teeple”.

Hawley spoke at Feucht’s Let Us Worship rally on the National Mall in October 2020, according to a Daily Caller video, and afterwards posted that it was a “huge privilege to be on the mall tonight with thousands and thousands of Christians gathered to worship and pray”.

There, Feucht led the crowd in prayer for Hawley, “calling on God to elevate ‘men and women of faith’ into positions of political power”, RNS reported at the time. Feucht’s channel also carries a video of Hawley addressing his Let Us Worship event in Washington in 2022.

The Guardian has previously reported on Canadian cities cancelling Feucht’s performances.

Teepell reportedly became Jindal’s chief of staff when Jindal took office as Louisiana governor in January 2008, and left the post in 2011 to become a partner at OnMessage. He managed Jindal’s 2016 presidential campaign, the Guardian reported in 2015.

OnMessage’s biography of Teepell, archived in 2019, describes him as Jindal’s “first chief of staff” and says he “served as lead consultant for Senator Josh Hawley’s upset victory over incumbent Democrat Senator Claire McCaskill” in 2018. Hawley’s campaign paid OnMessage $7,489,181 during that election cycle, FEC records show.

The younger Teepell joined Hawley’s Senate office as an intern in 2023 and rose to operations director before leaving in February, the Guardian reported on Monday, citing staff records. Before that, he was a part-time associate at OnMessage Inc from May 2020 to May 2023, according to his LinkedIn profile. After leaving Hawley’s office he became political director for Philip Sarnecki’s campaign for governor of Kansas. Sarnecki lost the Republican primary on 4 August.

Republicans have pressed the Muslim Brotherhood line against El-Sayed for several weeks. His opponent Mike Rogers, raised alleged Brotherhood ties during a debate, and Donald Trump has said without evidence that El-Sayed is “100%” Muslim Brotherhood. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has been involved with the group.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’

The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.

He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, saying the US move would save lives.

The Ukrainian president added: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”

The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needed a new leader.

The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.

Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”

He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.

Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.

Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.

“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”

The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.

Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.

The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.

“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.

Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.

US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.

At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: DoJ’s suspected non-citizens list includes ‘high percentage’ of those born in US, LA officials say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The statement revealed in court papers raises questions about the reliability of the list of 20,000 people in California

The justice department’s list of suspected non-citizens in California includes a “high percentage” of people born in the United States, Los Angeles election officials said on Tuesday.

The statement, made in court papers, raises further questions about the reliability of a list of 20,000 people the justice department provided to election officials in Los Angeles last week. The department sent the county and California secretary of state the list last week and gave them a 48-hour deadline to segregate ballots cast from anyone on the list unless they could verify their citizenship. California election officials refused and the Department of Justice sued them on Thursday.

Of the 20,000 names delivered to Los Angeles county, only about 7,000 people had an address in the county, according to the filing. Los Angeles officials analyzed a sample of 200 people on the list. “Among the records for which birthplace information was meaningfully reported, 38.9% indicated that they were born in the United States,” Aman Bhullar, an official in the Los Angeles clerk and recorder’s office, wrote in a court declaration. It is not immediately clear how many people that is and a county spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment.

Forty-three per cent of those on the list had a voter registration record that had been cancelled, Bhullar said in his declaration. Seventy-one per cent of those in the sample never voted, and 86 people had been mailed a ballot this year.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has compiled the list of non-citizens on the rolls, has resisted state demands to share its methodology for matching voter rolls for non-citizen records. Experts have warned that the way DHS is trying to match voter rolls to its own records could be error-prone.

Indeed, the DHS does not have a good track record so far. In July, it accused Nevada of having as many as 16,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls. DHS officials later sent Nevada election officials a list of 185 people it believed were non-citizens. Nevada officials responded by investigating the list and said all 185 were in fact citizens.

R Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, acknowledged during a press conference on Monday there could be citizens on the list.

“There may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens. We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us,” he said at a Monday press conference.

Kiersten Pels, a justice department spokesperson, said that just because someone listed a US birthplace on their voter registration form it didn’t mean they were a citizen.

“Just because an alien says on a form that they are a citizen doesn’t make them eligible to vote,” she said.

“California cannot facilitate the violation of federal law. We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn’t permit this willful blindness,” she added.

“I think she’s a sick, a very dishonest person, but who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It’s a real shit house,” he said.

Donald Trump was not optimistic about whether peace talks appear to be back on the table ahead of Steve Witkoff’s meeting in St Petersburg, Russia tomorrow (following his summit with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nordic leaders in Oslo).

“We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve got nothing back, other than high diesel,” Trump said, without acknowledging that the price of diesel and gasoline jumped at the beginning of the Iran war in February. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. In July, Fahima Egeh Mahamud, the CEO of the daycare center that appeared in Shirley’s video, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the US.

Under the administration’s proposed program, people who submit information through that results in a fraud conviction could receive up to $30,000.

In the Oval Office today, Trump presented Shirley, 24, with a check for $10,000 for his work.

Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 – does Adam Hamilton have the courage, brain and heart to cause an extraordinary upset?

Just two years after Donald Trump won Kansas by 16 points in his fight to regain the White House, Republicans in the state are scrambling to retain their dominance. The battle for one of its two seats in the US Senate is too close to call, setting the stage for a potentially extraordinary upset.

Some recent polls even put Democrat Adam Hamilton on course for a historic victory. Kansans have not sent a representative of the party to the US Senate since 1932.

On the campaign trail, Hamilton regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.

Washington needs more of all three, he says, and he can deliver it. He decided to run for office after seeing the Trump administration act in ways that were “not good or kind or compassionate or humble”, Hamilton – in the energetic cadence of the pastor he is – told a crowd of business leaders in Topeka on Friday. He was waiting for Roger Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent senator, to stand up for his state and its people.

“I would have arguments with Roger Marshall in the shower. He was not in the shower with me,” Hamilton joked. “And I would just say, Roger, please stand up for your people. You were not hired to be a spokesperson for the White House. You were hired to fight for your people.”

Hamilton’s role as senior pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation comes with name recognition and speaking skills. But Marshall’s liabilities as his opponent – namely, the fact he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them – have contributed greatly to Hamilton’s prospects of flipping the seat.

Electorally, he’s trying to win over independents and Republicans, calling himself an independent-minded Democrat. It would be valuable, he told the business leaders last week, for Kansas to have a Democrat like him and a Republican in Jerry Moran representing them in the US Senate – working both sides of the aisle.

Mike Bloomberg is donating $80m to Democrats ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Speaking to the New York Times on Tuesday, Bloomberg’s advisor Howard Wolfson said: “He believes in participation in our democracy. And obviously the scale of his participation, given his resources and his means, is greater than other people’s financially. But other people are participating in different ways.”

“He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns,” Wolfson said, adding that Bloomberg “expects a result.”

The outlet reports that the former New York City major, now 84-years old, is focused on securing a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives, with at least $50m of his doantion to be spent on House races.

In response to Bloomberg’s donation, House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries said: “Mayor Bloomberg played an incredibly instrumental role in the decisive midterm election in 2018. The extraordinary support from Mayor Bloomberg will once again help Democrats flip the House,” the outlet reports.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed

Italy’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting. Further demonstrations are planned on Saturday.

The government of the far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is also planning to swiftly approve tougher new security measures, including extending preventive detention for minors, cracking down on youth gangs and banning gatherings for people deemed a threat to public order, Italian media reported on Tuesday.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Tuesday some military forces would be deployed during ⁠protests ​planned for this Saturday, “mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order”.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told parliament that the police presence during Satuday’s demonstrations ⁠would be “massive” and that ​his ​goal was ​for an “immediate return ​to order” ‌after last weekend’s violent riots.

Police in Milan, in northern Italy, detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s cathedral, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.

Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

Images of Saturday’s clashes in France, including mobs looting shops and public buildings set on fire, prompted several countries including the US, China and Germany to issue travel advice for their citizens. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested in one of France’s most violent recent bouts of unrest.

French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice, and after a night of relative calm, Lecornu said on Tuesday that new curfews would be imposed where they were needed.

Authorities in Paris renewed Monday night’s curfew, which would apply from 11pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday to the Place de la République, where many of the weekend clashes took place, and in the central Les Halles shopping district.

Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, and banned masks and helmets in some areas. A man was also arrested in connection with the burning down of the historic town hall in Limoges.

The Italian press agency Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered in the country was aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known as maranza – a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually from marginalised areas.

Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.

Other stores ransacked included the sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and the mobile phone operator Vodafone, footage showed.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.

Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades after days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.

Meanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media. It said it would organise demonstrations there and in other Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.

“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”

Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.

There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview

Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.

Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.

“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”

In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.

“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”

“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.

The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against.

Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year are being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.

“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.

When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”

Kirby also maintained that fares are still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Ex-student alleging sexual assault felt ‘unsupported’ by Cornell president
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The ex-student writes she wants to share information that ‘may be relevant’ to vote of no confidence

The former Cornell University student who accused seven men of sexually assaulting her at a fraternity house in 2024 recently wrote a letter to campus faculty leaders saying that she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by the Ivy League institution’s president.

The letter addressed to the Cornell faculty senate was obtained and published by the New York Times on Tuesday – and in it the former student said she wanted to share information that she believed “may be relevant” as the panel considers a vote of no confidence in the school’s administration.

Identified in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, the student wrote that she was “sharing a second-hand account with you” of a comment the Cornell president, Michael Kotlikoff, had purportedly made during a meeting with the leader of her sorority at the time, Tri Delta. The comment was purported to have been made “shortly after my report of sexual assault to the university in 2024”, Jane Doe wrote.

Jane Doe said that she was told Kotlikoff’s “initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’”

A spokesperson for Cornell said in a statement on Tuesday that “the second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account.”

“The question ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024,” the spokesperson said. “He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”

In Jane Doe’s letter, which is two pages long and is dated 14 October, she wrote that the comments attributed to Kotlikoff and reported to her “diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school”.

She also wrote that her sorority president had shared the conversation with her “with concern” – and that her sorority sister had “interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story”.

“When the then-Tri Delta President relayed this conversation to me, I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” the former student wrote. “I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the faculty senate are among them.”

She added: “I would not want to withhold something potentially pertinent, only for Senate members to later discover that information relevant to their deliberations had not been made available to them.”

According to the Times, the meeting that the former student is referring to in the letter took place in January 2025.

The faculty senate scheduled a 28 October meeting to debate the no-confidence resolution – “followed by electronic voting”, according to the group’s website.

It comes as Cornell’s administration has faced backlash and criticism for its handling of the 2024 allegations that were made public in a civil lawsuit filed by the former student in September against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its former brothers, and her sorority.

In the lawsuit, Jane Doe accused seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.

It has been reported that the woman first reported the case to the Cornell University police department in November 2024. According to records obtained by the Times, after an internal investigation at Cornell, two of the men were expelled, two were suspended, and another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus.

The remaining men received lighter punishments, which included an order to not contact Jane Doe, and to write “reflection papers”.

In an interview with the Times published on 13 October, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he knew a student had reported being sexually assaulted in November 2024 – but did not follow up with Jane Doe involved in the months afterward.

Kotlikoff, who has described the allegations as “deeply disturbing”, said that he and other school officials did not have the full picture of Jane Doe’s allegations and the subsequent investigation until earlier in October.

Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.

Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.

“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.

The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Great white shark leaps from water and photobombs California beachgoers
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Videos show shark launching several feet from water as a group of friends pose for photos along Marina state beach

A great white shark put on a spectacular display for California beachgoers over the weekend, leaping from the water off Marina state beach and photobombing visitors.

Videos circulating online show a great white shark launching several feet out of the water in the background as a group of friends pose for photos along the beach.

In a statement to the Guardian, California state park officials said: “California State Parks independently confirmed a shark matching the characteristics of a great white [breached] off the shore near Marina State Beach at the same time as the video.

“Posted shark notices are in effect at the beach in accordance with the department’s protocol. State Parks would like to remind visitors that sharks are an important part of the coastal ecosystem and that interactions between people and sharks are rare,” the officials added.

Great white sharks frequent Monterey Bay seasonally, traveling to offshore waters near Hawaii before returning to California’s coast in late summer and early fall. The Central Coast provides important habitat for the predators, which feed on fish and marine mammals, including seals.

In recent years, great white shark sightings have increased along parts of the west coast, with changing ocean conditions amid the climate crisis influencing their migratory patterns.

El Niño events, which can bring marine heatwaves and warmer-than-usual ocean temperatures, can disrupt marine ecosystems, prompting cold-water species such as the great white to shift northward or move into deeper waters in search of cooler temperatures.

Classified as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), great white sharks can grow up to 20ft (6 metres) long and weigh as much as 4,000lb (1,800kg) . As apex predators and keystone species, they play a vital role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems by regulating prey populations, redistributing nutrients and helping limit the spread of disease by consuming sick or injured prey.

Yet despite their critical ecological roles, great whites have long been misrepresented as man-eating predators, a portrayal popularized by films such as Jaws that have threatened their conservation.

Despite their fearsome reputation, the species has faced steep population declines, exceeding 90% in some regions during the 20th century. Recreational and commercial fishing, by-catch, illegal poaching and trafficking, habitat degradation and the climate crisis continue to threaten their survival.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 – does Adam Hamilton have the courage, brain and heart to cause an extraordinary upset?

Just two years after Donald Trump won Kansas by 16 points in his fight to regain the White House, Republicans in the state are scrambling to retain their dominance. The battle for one of its two seats in the US Senate is too close to call, setting the stage for a potentially extraordinary upset.

Some recent polls even put Democrat Adam Hamilton on course for a historic victory. Kansans have not sent a representative of the party to the US Senate since 1932.

On the campaign trail, Hamilton regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.

Washington needs more of all three, he says, and he can deliver it. He decided to run for office after seeing the Trump administration act in ways that were “not good or kind or compassionate or humble”, Hamilton – in the energetic cadence of the pastor he is – told a crowd of business leaders in Topeka on Friday. He was waiting for Roger Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent senator, to stand up for his state and its people.

“I would have arguments with Roger Marshall in the shower. He was not in the shower with me,” Hamilton joked. “And I would just say, Roger, please stand up for your people. You were not hired to be a spokesperson for the White House. You were hired to fight for your people.”

Hamilton’s role as senior pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation comes with name recognition and speaking skills. But Marshall’s liabilities as his opponent – namely, the fact he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them – have contributed greatly to Hamilton’s prospects of flipping the seat.

He readily and frequently shares the stories of everyday Kansans he’s met on the trail for US Senate, from the woman whose health insurance premiums cost as much as her mortgage, so she had to drop coverage, to the farmer who cried over the state of the industry for young farmers.

Electorally, he’s trying to win over independents and Republicans, calling himself an independent-minded Democrat. It would be valuable, he told the business leaders last week, for Kansas to have a Democrat like him and a Republican in Jerry Moran representing them in the US Senate – working both sides of the aisle.

In a video welcoming Trump to Kansas, Hamilton said he hoped the president would hear from the people struggling throughout Kansas with rising costs and uncertainty. But, he told Kansans, they all had a place in his campaign, regardless of who they voted for, or their party affiliation.

“I’m running to be a champion for the people of Kansas: Republicans, Democrats and independents. I won’t answer to a party, and I won’t answer to any one person in Washington,” he said in the video. “I answer to you.”

In Topeka, Kansas voters were open to the pitch. Several who attended Hamilton’s forum on Friday had attended a similar forum with Marshall earlier in the day. Before and after the event, Hamilton circulated through the crowd of a few dozen voters, shaking hands and taking photos. Voters said they appreciated his accessibility, even if some wanted some more specific answers.

Brennen Ross, a 20-year-old political science and economics student at Washburn University in Topeka, watched Marshall earlier in the day then came to see Hamilton. The national attention on Kansas now has been “super interesting” for a state often best known for its sports teams, he said.

He’s an unaffiliated voter, leaning toward Hamilton. The cost of housing, the job market for people his age and the availability of water in rural Kansas are all weighing on his mind, he said. The first issue he mentioned, though, was Hamilton’s effort to “turn the heat down” amid rising political polarization.

“That’s really compelling, and it resonates with a lot of Kansans, especially like a lot of younger Kansans that I speak to on this election,” Ross said.

Jacinta Bergkamp, a 30-year-old Democrat with a young professional group called Forge Young Talent, asked both Hamilton and Marshall about housing affordability at each of their events. She said affordability looms large across the board for young people. Women’s rights and access to abortion matter to her vote, too.

Bergkamp, wearing a shirt that said “Vote Dammit”, has found the Democratic interest in Kansas “encouraging” and said that Kansans have seemed “fed up” with what they’re experiencing, with more people willing to speak out against their representatives and hold them accountable.

“Usually it feels a little, I guess, lonely” to be a Democrat in Kansas, she said. “We always kind of think of Kansas as being purple. Kansas isn’t red or blue … It’s very clear that Kansas is more liberal than what people think outside of Kansas.”

Linda Murphy Maina, who owns a Topeka boutique called Linda’s Afrikan Kreations, said she looks for which candidates are good for the people, and how they can serve the community. On some questions, she wanted more direct answers, but she felt Hamilton homed in on working together and helping people. “I’m still doing a little research, but he tickled my fancy,” she said.

Susana Ortiz, a counselor who has a private practice in Topeka, said her background in mental health meant she looks for candidates who would be best for her clients. She doesn’t expect candidates to have all the answers, but they need to show they care about people, and are willing to accept feedback from the public about their decisions.

Ortiz is still deciding who to vote for. “More and more people, it seems, are expressing frustration with the rising cost of living,” she said. “And so they’re looking for solutions, and I think that allows people to be a little more open-minded to perhaps voting across party lines.”

Hamilton, working to convince the politically mixed crowd to take a chance on a Democrat, told the Topeka business leaders that he didn’t think Marshall had done a good job of listening to the people. He noted that the last time Marshall held an open town hall was about 600 days ago, when he left the town hall after facing pointed questions. (Marshall has said the town halls became “non-productive and dangerous”.)

Hamilton doesn’t have many superpowers, he told the crowd. He can’t sing, he’s bad at golf, he was a horrible football player. His superpower, he said, is that he listens and he really cares, and he has a “propensity to fight for people”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It’s the most heartbreaking thing’: the active-duty soldiers who have to visit Texas food banks
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Nearly half of enlisted families struggled to afford enough food last year. Congress has known for decades how to solve the problem

This article was produced with the Food & Environment Reporting Network, and supported by the Economic Hardship Reporting Project

The Armed Services YMCA in Harker Heights, Texas, is a state-of-the-art facility, with a swimming pool, gym and coffee shop. There’s also a food pantry tucked away in a small room at the far end of a hallway on the second floor, where active-duty soldiers stationed nearby at Fort Hood can receive free groceries. More than a dozen pantries surround the army base, where about 40,000 soldiers are stationed.

The pantry’s parking lot is where I found Miguel Pérez on a July morning, lugging a heavy reusable grocery bag to his pickup under the already blazing central Texas sun.

Pérez, a 39-year-old army combat engineer, was on leave and asked that I not use his real name. His bag contained sweet potatoes, a box of elbow macaroni, a 5lb bag of frozen chicken breasts, some enormous beets, a dozen eggs and a few other staples – about $100 worth of food by his reckoning.

Born in the Dominican Republic, Pérez lived in Colorado and worked in casinos before losing his job during the Covid-19 pandemic. A friend who worked as an army recruiter suggested he look into the military. He was 34 when he enlisted, completing basic training at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, and eventually landing at Fort Hood.

Combat engineers are responsible for emplacing and destroying obstacles on behalf of infantry and tank units. It’s dangerous work, involving explosives and grueling physical labor, but Pérez said he was happy in the army. “I always wanted to do this,” he said.

Still, constant financial stress has made an already difficult job even harder. Military pay breaks down into several main categories, including base pay, housing allowance, food allowance, and dozens of minor supplements for things like hazardous duty, combat, demolition, diving and aviation. Pay also depends on rank and time in service. Pérez, who joined five years ago and has earned the rank of sergeant, said he brings home about $4,800 a month, including about $1,600 for housing and $476 for food – or just shy of $58,000 a year. “In the military we don’t make that much to cover gas, housing, kids’ back-to-school costs, utilities,” he said. “It’s hard today for us.”

Pérez usually visits the ASYMCA pantry twice a month, shaving about $200 from his monthly grocery bill. “When you come early, you see a lot of military people,” he said. “We need it.”

As a sergeant responsible for several younger soldiers, Pérez said he had seen how shame deters troops from seeking assistance. “They look at it like if you’re taking something for free to eat, it’s a bad thing,” he said. “I guess they’re embarrassed about it.”

Reluctance to seek help can obscure how widespread the problem has become. Nationwide, nearly half of all active-duty military families experienced food insecurity in 2025, according to research from the non-profit Military Family Advisory Network – more than double the rate in 2023. The ASYMCA’s food distribution programs, which serve more than 50 military installations, saw a 23% jump in demand last year. The problem is especially acute among the enlisted ranks, with almost 57% reporting food insecurity last year, compared with 14% of officers.

Lower-ranking troops with families are the hardest hit. One out of every five active-duty families reported eating “less than they felt they should because there wasn’t enough money for food in the past year”, according to a similar study by the non-profit Blue Star Families.

Instead of getting help, Pérez said, some soldiers make difficult choices about where to allocate their limited funds. One of his soldiers got a speeding ticket and told Pérez: “I can’t pay it, because if I pay it, I’m not gonna buy groceries.”

Pérez’s finances took a hit after a recent divorce, when he became the sole provider for his two sons, a 16-year-old and a three-year-old. Like many troops living off base, his $1,900 monthly rent outstrips his housing allowance, which means he’s paying part of his rent out of his base pay. After covering all of his expenses, there’s little margin for error – and his case is typical.

According to Sheri Yerrington, executive director of the Killeen ASYMCA – which serves the Fort Hood area – demand for food assistance has grown steadily since the pantry opened three years ago. “It’s been anywhere from a 12-19% increase every year,” she said. In 2025, the Killeen ASYMCA delivered 500,000lb of food to more than 19,000 families. About 80% of the Killeen pantry’s customers are active-duty military personnel and their families. Open every Thursday, the pantry often runs out of food by the early afternoon.

“It’s the most heartbreaking thing for a soldier in uniform to walk in here at one o’clock and our pantry is already empty, and I have to turn them away,” Yerrington said. “That is the worst feeling, and I have had it.”

Shocking as it may seem to people who have never relied on a military paycheck, food insecurity among active-duty troops has been a problem for decades.

The reason is clear: military pay is insufficient for many enlisted families. The Gates Commission – appointed by President Richard Nixon in 1969 to study the feasibility of ending the draft and transitioning to an all-volunteer force – highlighted the “inequity” of military pay, compared with civilian wages, as a likely barrier to recruitment.

For a few years in the 1970s, increases in military pay for the junior ranks outpaced wage growth for comparable civilian jobs. As members of the newly minted all-volunteer force grew up and started families, flaws in the structure of military pay emerged.

By the late 1990s, Senator John McCain, a Republican and a veteran, was railing against the fact that tens of thousands of soldiers were collecting food stamps, calling it a “national disgrace”. In 2000, he authored a bill to provide service members eligible for food stamps with a monthly nutritional allowance in their military paycheck. “We must end the days of a ‘food-stamp Army’ once and for all,” he said.

McCain’s bill failed, but it inspired a mandate in the 2001 National Defense Authorization Act that the basic allowance for subsistence be included in every military member’s paycheck as a standard allowance. McCain’s bill also led to the creation of the family subsistence supplemental allowance, which was designed to raise qualifying military families’ income to 130% of the federal poverty level. (In 2002, that was $18,100 for a family of four. By 2026, inflation had raised it to $33,000.)

The program was a failure, bogged down by restrictive criteria and a complicated approval process. Few families applied, and of those who did, almost all were rejected. In 2013 – when 620,000 military households sought some kind of food assistance and “nearly $104 million worth of food stamps were used at military commissaries”, according to the military news outlet Task & Purpose – the FSSA program denied 97% of applicants. The program was discontinued in 2016.

The failure of the FSSA showed that the military’s financial assistance programs often exclude the service members who need them most. The same is true for federal programs outside the military. For example, the Department of Agriculture, which administers the Snap program, counts basic allowance for housing – a stipend provided to troops living off-base to offset local housing costs – toward household income. Because housing allowance is pegged to local rental rates, it often pushes a military family’s income above the Snap eligibility threshold, especially in high-cost markets such as California, Hawaii and Alaska.

According to Liza Lieberman, vice-president of communications at the non-profit Mazon, an anti-hunger organization, the inclusion of the housing allowance as income amounts to an administrative barrier that locks troops out of Snap. “They never see that money,” she said.

For five years, Congress stalled on creating a replacement for the defunct FSSA. “There were Republicans and Democrats on the hill that were laughing us out of the room,” said Lieberman, who advocated for an improved program to address military food insecurity. “No one wanted to acknowledge or confront the fact that we were not paying our troops enough.”

In 2021, Congress finally approved a new program called the basic needs allowance, which is now available – in theory – to service members with dependents whose annual income is less than 200% of the federal poverty level. But the approval process remains confusing and time-consuming, according to Lieberman. The new program also requires troops to apply through their chain of command, which can be intimidating and embarrassing, especially for troops worried that appearing financially irresponsible might negatively affect promotion. The military does not publish data related to enrollment in the basic needs allowance, but in 2023 – its first year – only 77 families received the supplement.

Most years, Congress approves a modest increase in military pay to keep pace with cost of living increases, usually between 1% and 4%. In 2025, the Senate approved an exceptional 14.5% pay increase for the junior enlisted ranks and a 4.5% increase for all other troops. Consecutive pay increases brought the average base salary of an enlistee with less than two years of service from about $22,000 in 2022 to nearly $28,000 in 2025, according to USAFacts, a non-profit that analyzes government data. But inflation and sharply escalating living costs have neutralized a large portion of those gains. “There’s a misconception that they got a pay raise, so the issue is resolved,” said Lieberman, “but the cost of groceries and gas have also increased.”

Childcare costs have increased more than 36% since 2019, residential rents are up by about 40% and vehicle insurance has surged by 48%. The cost of energy has jumped 16% in the past year alone, with gasoline prices spiking about 40% since the start of Trump’s war on Iran in February.

Housing allowances are supposed to be pegged to local rental markets, but rents have soared nationwide in recent years, which means that military personnel with families are often required to dig into their base pay to cover the gap, as in Pérez’s case. The problem is getting worse: according to a report from the army’s Directorate of Prevention, Resilience and Readiness, only 37% of soldiers were able to find housing within the limits of their allowance in 2025, down from 58% in 2020.

According to Shannon Razsadin, co-founder and CEO of the Military Families Advisory Network, the perennial insufficiency of military pay – even with need-based supplements and periodic pay raises – speaks to a more fundamental problem. “The reality is that the military compensation structure is not designed to sustain a full household,” she said. Instead, she explained, it was designed to support 18-year-old single enlistees living in barracks and eating at dining facilities. Today, Razsadin said, many recruits enter the service with spouses, young children and sometimes extended family members depending on them.
