In a country that treats workers as expendable parts, Hurts’s playing through a blood clot is just the highest-profile example of the price workers pay in an oligarchy.

The Philadelphia Eagles’s Jalen Hurts during the NFL match between the Eagles and the Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 11, 2026, in London, United Kingdom.

In a world where the attention spans of sports commentators and fans are roughly the same as that of a cat chasing a laser pointer, sometimes a story breaks through that demands our undivided attention. Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts could have died this week, and, despite the relentless churn of the news cycle, we must not look away.

The 2025 Super Bowl MVP was told by the Eagles’ medical staff that he had a “superficial blood clot” after an opponent’s cleat smashed into his calf on October 8. Hurts found himself the night before game day in a London hospital until 3 am, where he was told that sleeping could cause the clot to spread and risk his life. Hurts then, according to reports, attempted to pull an all-nighter, though he may have taken a nap at the stadium before game time—this part of the story is unclear. He then played in the game, where he attempted 40 passes. The Eagles lost 19–17, and Hurts took another transatlantic flight home. After he attended practice for another two days, an ultrasound revealed that Hurts’s condition had worsened. He was diagnosed with deep-vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning he now had multiple blood clots in both lungs. Hurts is out for the season, taking blood thinners, and fortunate that he avoided a pulmonary embolism.

When the story first broke, “NFL insider” Tom Pelissero had the following hot take: “How committed is Jalen Hurts to football?”

So committed, Pelissero wrote, that “after initially being diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in London, doctors told him not to sleep as a precaution, so he had been awake for roughly 36 hours when he started against the Jaguars, throwing for 220 yards and a TD.” (Pelissero later walked back the “awake for 36 hours” part, which was disputed by Hurts’s agent.)

It’s exactly that kind of tough-guy “committed to football” narrative that puts Hurts’s life—and the health of all players—at risk. As former NFLPA chief DeMaurice Smith would remind people, “This is the only job with a 100 percent injury rate.” These injuries invariably get exacerbated because football players, with their non-guaranteed contracts, will always play unless stopped. This is more than a financial concern. It is built into the toxic, gladiator ethos of the sport.

But moments like these are precisely when a team’s medical staff is supposed to intervene. Without their involvement, coaches will do whatever they need to do to keep their jobs, and a quarterback willing to go through a wall to win a game will agree to it, even if it means playing with a blood clot in front of an indifferent London crowd. This is especially the case in Philadelphia, where the Eagles’ perpetually enraged fans were already calling for Coach Nick Sirianni’s job—despite his winning the Super Bowl just 20 months before—because of an early-season losing streak.

What happened with Hurts also makes one wonder where the NFL Players Association, the union that represents players, was as this news broke across the sports world. It should be up in arms, demanding answers for how this could have possibly taken place. Instead, it’s MIA, having not put out—as of this writing—even a boilerplate statement about health and safety guidelines or how players must be protected. The Nation has received no comment from the union, but I have received messages from former players frustrated that it has become so toothless and unwilling, even rhetorically, to shout from the rooftops that such an incident is utterly unacceptable.

The Hurts story feels bigger than one player avoiding a fatal tragedy. It is a microcosm of larger issues within the league, which treats its players—even star quarterbacks—as equipment. These aren’t “gladiators.” They are workers: workers whose average career is three and a half years. The league, despite all of its rhetoric about player safety, treats them like they’re disposable.

But the Hurts microcosm doesn’t end on the football field. This is about a worker who risked his life, with the approval of company doctors, and without the assistance of a union, which chose instead to cover its eyes and ears as long as the National Football League’s golden goose of app gambling and streaming services keeps laying eggs. In a country that treats workers as expendable parts of a production line, with many unions unworthy of the struggles that created them in the first place, Jalen Hurts is just the highest-profile example of the price workers pay in an oligarchy. In this oligarchy, private-equity overlords in the owners’ box look down on their expensive toys and think of themselves as the emperors of ancient Rome. In reality, they represent the worst of us, watching others inflict pain for their own profit and amusement.

Jalen Hurts deserved better than this. So do the rest of us. Now the NFL and its media partners are trying to move on to the next topic, hoping our addiction to gambling and Fantasy Sports will allow us to “thingify” and dehumanize Hurts enough that we can still enjoy the spectacle without considering the price paid. We can’t let them. This is a story of corporate and medical malfeasance, which is also a story too many of us know all too well in a country where cruelty has become more than “the point.” It has become currency.

Dave Zirin is the sports editor at The Nation. He is the author of 11 books on the politics of sports. He is the author of a new book, The People's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Terrifying Future of States’ Criminalizing Pregnant People Is Already Here
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The idea of charging people who have abortions with murder is gaining traction on the right. But a report finds that people are already being prosecuted for their pregnancy outcomes.

Anti-abortion rights demonstrators march to the Supreme Court for the 52nd annual March For Life in Washington, DC, on January 24, 2025.

Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, the idea of charging people who have abortions with murder has gained terrifying new traction. During her brief stint as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia became just the latest prominent conservative to draw attention for her ties to a radical wing of the anti-abortion movement that wants to charge people who have abortions with murder. This year alone, state lawmakers floated 14 bills to charge people who have abortions with homicide. (The idea is still so unpopular across the political spectrum that none of those bills passed.) Yet this whole debate is, in a sense, a red herring, because hundreds of people a year are already being prosecuted for their pregnancy outcomes. The vast majority of those cases involved a live birth where the mother was suspected of using drugs, but in a rising minority of cases since Dobbs, people are also being criminalized for pregnancy loss.

I spoke with Dana Sussman, senior vice president at Pregnancy Justice, about a report the organization published today finding that in the first three years after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, prosecutors have initiated at least 902 cases across the country charging individuals with crimes related to pregnancy, pregnancy loss, or birth.

Amy Littlefield: What’s new in this report, which looks at pregnancy criminalization in the first three years after Dobbs?

Dana Sussman: When Roe was overturned, we suspected that pregnancy loss would become an increasingly criminally suspect event, and we unfortunately are starting to see that play out in the data. This report finds a significant acceleration in pregnancy loss prosecutions. We now have documented 70 pregnancy loss prosecutions in the first three years post-Dobbs.

AL: I was struck by the breakdown of allegations prosecutors made in the cases you found. There were 871 allegations of substance use during pregnancy, 77 allegations of a lack of prenatal care, and just 13 related to obtaining, attempting or researching an abortion. What does this tell us about who is being criminalized for pregnancy post-Dobbs?

DS: This is the continuation of a trend that we’ve been seeing for decades. The way that pregnancy is policed and prosecuted in the United States is through the lens of substance use. The foundation for prosecuting pregnancy is based in the war on drugs from the 1980s, and the way in which Black women, in particular, were targeted for charges of child abuse when they were deemed substance users, primarily with crack cocaine and this obsession over a “crack baby epidemic” that has been thoroughly debunked. Three state supreme court decisions used pregnancy and substance use as the way to redefine who a person is [thereby extending child abuse protections to fetuses] under their state laws: Alabama, South Carolina, and Oklahoma, which consistently rank among the top three states that criminalize pregnancy.

AL: What did you find about the race and socioeconomic background of the folks who were criminalized for their pregnancy outcomes in this report?

DS: In the ’80s, ’90s, and early 2000s, we were seeing disproportionately Black women being charged with crimes in connection with pregnancy, and that has shifted since the mid-2000s until the present. The majority are white women at this point, but poverty is a very big indicator, as it is across the criminal justice system. So we’re looking at poor white women as the majority in the data set at this point. There are a few different theories from scholars about why this is. [Legal scholar] Michele Goodwin has said that Black women were the canary in the coal mine; cruelty by the state is tried out on Black women, and then it spreads more broadly. There’s also a lot of scholarship showing that when a victim is white, the perpetrator of the crime is treated more harshly, and so we are talking about the assumption that these are white babies, and so they are held in higher esteem, frankly, than non-white babies, and so their mothers are treated more harshly, potentially. There’s also shifting patterns in policing around nonviolent drug crimes; we see less of it in city centers and more of it in rural areas, and also the patterns of drug use, as well.

AL: So it’s mostly low-income white women in a small number of states. I’m looking at the map: 381 of the cases in South Carolina, 222 in Oklahoma, 204 in Alabama, and then there’s states like my home state of Massachusetts where there’s zero.

DS: Each one of those three states has proclaimed by state supreme court decision that fetuses are children under the child abuse laws. In South Carolina, it was in the late ’90s; in Alabama, it was 2013; and in Oklahoma, it was 2020. So that kind of unleashed permission for prosecutors across the state to apply laws in this way. In other states, we see prosecutors doing this, but those cases have not yet gone to the state supreme court. In Mississippi, for example, the state has no fetal personhood law or judicial decision, and yet we see 27 cases in that state of prosecutors just choosing to reinterpret laws that were never intended to be applied in this way.

AL: So what impact did Dobbs actually have on these types of prosecutions, and is Dobbs really the culprit here, or are there other, more long-standing forces at play?

DS: Two things are true here. One is that the foundation for these prosecutions was laid way before Dobbs, and it’s a continuation of a decades-long trend. Fetal personhood is at the root of these cases, and fetal personhood has existed in state law or in state judicial decisions since the 1990s. That is, ultimately, the anti-abortion movement’s goal. It wasn’t the overturning of Roe. It wasn’t sending issues back to the states. It is the federalization of fetal and embryonic personhood, because that would ban abortion without question, without exception, and it would allow for increased criminalization of people who are not performing pregnancy in the way that the powers that be might want them to. At the same time, we suspect that we are seeing more pregnancy loss cases in our data year upon year post-Dobbs, and I don’t think that should be a surprise, either. If we ban abortion and we make pregnancy loss suspicious because in some places provision of abortion has been made illegal, then we are creating an environment in which we are inviting law enforcement in to investigate how some of these pregnancies ended. That criminal response varies depending on one’s identity, one’s behavior, and one’s access to healthcare.

AL: After the Supreme Court decision in Dobbs in 2022, there were predictions that we would see a mass number of criminal cases related to abortion, because all of a sudden providing abortion was a crime in about a dozen states. How does the reality compare to those expectations?

DS: We are seeing what we expected: that this was going to fall most harshly on people who use substances during pregnancy and were going to be charged with child abuse or neglect, and that pregnancy loss would be an increasingly suspect event. I remember getting lots of questions about period-tracking apps and wiping that from your phone, and I was like, if they want to criminalize pregnancy, they have other ways to do it, and they’ve been doing it. This is not going to be some new dragnet, it’s going to be the same old ways that they’ve been doing it for a very long time, and that has played out. And the circumstances are often through healthcare, that is, the people who are reporting to law enforcement or child welfare [are often healthcare providers]. That was the case before Dobbs, and it remains the case now.

AL: Katie Zacharia recently made headlines for the fact that she was on the board of White Rose Resistance, which is part of an extreme wing of the anti-abortion movement that has called for “equal protection” laws that would treat embryos as people and abortions as murder. I’m wondering if you could reflect on the fears generated by these efforts versus what the data already show about criminalization?

DS: There are 17 states that redefine who a person is to include an embryo or a fetus right now. So this movement to provide “equal protection” to embryos and fetuses already exists in a slightly different form under many state laws.

AL: What would you tell someone who lives in a state where abortion is banned, and is ordering abortion pills to self-manage an abortion?

DS: These are an incredibly small number of cases [criminalizing self-managed abortion in a ban state] when it comes to how many abortions have happened post-Dobbs. You can still access abortion safely and confidentially, and if you are experiencing medical concerns around abortion care, you can call the Miscarriage and Abortion Hotline. You can get care that you need and you do not need to say anything about abortion. People should keep their community of people who know as small and as trusted as possible, because the most common scenario [triggering criminal prosecution] is getting reported by other people.

Amy Littlefield is The Nation’s abortion access correspondent and a journalist who focuses on reproductive rights, healthcare, and religion. Her latest book is Killers of Roe: My Investigation Into the Mysterious Death of Abortion Rights (Hachette).

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Supreme Court Is Coming for Affirmative Action—Again
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The high court has just accepted a case that takes aim at efforts to increase diversity at high-performing public schools.

One might think that mediocre white folks and the minority of AAPI parents who have decided to join forces with them would be happy after their victory over affirmative action in the 2023 case known as Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard. They succeeded in their goal of reinterpreting the 14th Amendment as “colorblind”—notwithstanding the fact that the 14th Amendment was a direct response to over 200 years of slavery and oppression of Black people in the New World—and with it ushered in a new era of “white makes right” hiring practices.

The SFFA case has been extremely effective at limiting opportunities for Black and Latino students. Enrollment at the top 50 most selective colleges and universities plummeted for Black students during the year after the Supreme Court’s decision, falling by 27 percent. Enrollment for Latinos fell 10 percent. These people have won.

And yet, the winners are not happy or satisfied. They feel they haven’t won enough, especially the people on the Supreme Court who are primarily responsible for making it harder for Black and Latino students to get into school. Having succeeded in cratering enrollment in colleges and universities, the court has moved on to its next target… fifth graders. Apparently, some Black and Latino fifth graders dared to get accepted into a few middle schools in Maryland and, well, parents of white and AAPI children can’t have that, now can they?

On Monday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case arose when a group of mostly Asian American parents sued a Maryland school district over its admissions process for four highly selective magnet schools.

The policy, adopted in 2021, during the Covid pandemic, involved placing all fifth graders who met a set of criteria—grades, reading comprehension, and, yes, the beloved standardized test scores—into a pool. The kids’ scores were compared with other kids’ scores at similar elementary schools (for instance, children who came from schools with high poverty rates were compared with other children from schools with high poverty rates). From within that pool, students were then chosen randomly to attend one of the four magnet schools. It makes sense that kids should be compared with other kids from similar schools in order to get into the pool of potential lottery winners, since how you do relative to the educational environment you find yourself in should be the thing that matters when we’re talking about freaking elementary school. But if you think like that, then you’re not thinking like a parent who is sure that any opportunity that goes to a kid who is not their own is an affront to the natural order of racial supremacy and the Constitution.

In any case, during the time period this plan was active, AAPI enrollment actually went up at two of the four schools, and AAPI students were overrepresented in the magnet schools relative to their population in Montgomery County.

So you have ostensibly “race-neutral” criteria. You have a literal random lottery. You have enrollment going up for AAPI students in some schools, but the Maryland schools were still occasionally admitting the Black and Latino fifth graders by allowing those kids to compete against their peers instead of on an unequal playing field, so that meant some Asian American parents could still be pissed off enough to file a lawsuit.

While we’re here, I think it’s important to point out that, although I certainly blame the litigating parents for their participation in racial discrimination against kids from impoverished schools, I am able to see why they think they have to drip this bile over other people’s children. It is, fundamentally, ridiculous that we are made to think there are only four good middle schools in an entire county. Why isn’t every school as good and desirable as these four magnet schools? Why do we make parents feel like educational resources are scarce and must be competed for in a zero-sum environment.

One solution to the problem of equal opportunity in education is to make every school a palace. Getting into a good school shouldn’t be like winning a lottery. It should be the default expectation in this society. But… we don’t want to do that. We’d rather send AAPI kids and Black kids and Latino kids and even white kids into some kind of Dickensian tragedy where there’s not enough education to go around so some kids get gruel.

Be that as it may, the lawsuit was dismissed by the lower courts because, obviously, when you have race-neutral criteria, a literal lottery, and your group does better than its proportional representation, it’s pretty hard to allege racial discrimination against you with a straight face. Moreover, the lawsuit should be moot because the Montgomery Board of Education uses some other system now. There’s no reason for the Supreme Court to take up the case other than to overrule the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals,

For a mercy, I guess, the Supreme Court seems only to be interested in a narrow question: whether the fact that the system was race-neutral is enough to dismiss a claim for discrimination against AAPI students out of hand. My guess is that the Republican supermajority will say “no,” and that the case will therefore move forward, allowing the lawyers to keep searching for evidence that Black fifth graders shouldn’t get into magnet schools as long as there is a white or Asian kid who wants to go to the same school.

But in some sense, that’s the most dangerous part of a lawsuit—the fact that, despite victory, the victors are not satisfied and will not be satisfied until Black students are drummed out of the system. We see the strands of this kind of mentality from the functional spokesperson for the entire white and AAPI grievance movement, legal gadfly Ed Blum. On Monday, Blum was given an entire column in Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post to argue that colleges and universities are still discriminating against white and AAPI students by admitting Black people. Blum’s main point of contention was, as always, test scores: “The median LSAT scores of rejected Asian and White applicants in the 2024-2025 cycle at Duke far exceeded the median scores of admitted Black applicants, who were 3½ times more likely to be admitted than a similarly qualified Asian applicant,” Blum wrote. He then went on to decry the fact that schools (Blum’s column was mostly focused on law schools) continue to use personal essays and other factors to make admissions decisions.

People like Blum would have you believe that standardized test scores are the only thing that should matter when it comes to admissions—as if every applicant in the country should take a test and the person who scores “the best” should get into their first-choice school and so on and so forth, until the person who scores the worst can either go to Trump University or kill themselves.

But that’s not how admissions have ever worked or should ever work. Schools are going to take a number of factors into account when building their applicant pool. Blum, who has pushed these cases and organized groups of AAPI parents to do the same, has succeeded in convincing the courts that race is the one factor, different from all others, that schools cannot look at—but admissions committees are still free (as of now, at least) to look at a number of other things, including: geographic distribution, gender, economic factors, leadership qualities, legacy status, and whether an applicant “fits” with the school’s mission and ethos. Some law schools, for instance, place a heavy emphasis on work experience; others value people who are likely to stay local and serve the community where the school is located. Blum sees only one test to rule them all, but people smarter than Blum appreciate the (trigger warning) diversity of an admitted class with a mix of skills and strengths to bring to the classroom.

Blum’s solution to the apparent problem that Black people are still getting into school despite his organization’s best efforts is Orwellian in scope. He demands “mandatory public disclosure” of all of a school’s applicants. “This would include,” he wrote, “standardized test scores, GPAs, family income, Pell Grant eligibility, AP coursework and other metrics, broken down by race and ethnicity.”

Can you imagine applying to a school and, as a result, watching your family’s personal income become a matter of public record? Can you imagine having to share whether or not you are eligible for a Pell Grant with the entire world? Can you imagine having to do all of this because some guy like Ed Blum doesn’t think you belong in school? In three years, Blum has gone from “universities shouldn’t consider race” to “universities should make public personal information, broken down by race and ethnicity, for my edification.”

The goal isn’t just to keep Black and Latino kids out of schools; it’s to discourage them and their parents from even applying. It’s not enough that Black and Latino enrollment should fall off a cliff. If there is one Black kid in a selective school, there’s a white or AAPI parent who thinks their kid should have gotten in instead. No matter that the white or AAPI kid couldn’t outcompete a kid with similar education privileges who did get in. No matter that a test score isn’t the only or best measure of a person’s academic worth or intellectual potential. If a Black or Latino kid exists at a school, people like Ed Blum will always argue that they shouldn’t.

For these people, one Black kid will always be one too many. They think the Constitution doesn’t protect equal protection and equal access to opportunity. They think it protects overrepresentation for their kids.
