https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: California to receive $6m settlement after 23andMe data breach
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Millions of customers’ genetic and personal information exposed in 2023, including more than 855,000 Californians

California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, on Monday announced the state will receive a $6m settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ ⁠genetic and other ⁠personal information.

California had ​unsuccessfully tried to block the $305m sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a non-profit controlled by the 23andMe ⁠co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California’s Genetic Information Privacy Act, and it had said ⁠consumers did not give express consent to the sale.

Once a trailblazer in DNA testing ​kits, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in ‌March 2025, seeking to ‌sell its business at auction after a decline in demand and legal ‌fallout from the data breach.

A US bankruptcy judge ruled against California’s objections to the sale, and later ruled that the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company’s successor. California lost an appeal over the sale in federal district court, and it agreed to drop further appeals as ‌part of the $6m settlement, according to court documents filed on Monday.

Customers of 23andMe retained the option to delete their data during ​the bankruptcy sale process, but California had argued that the court should have disallowed the transfer of any data unless 23andMe customers first gave express consent to the sale.

“I am proud to fight for the privacy rights of Californians and to ⁠deliver this settlement for consumers who put their trust in 23andMe,” ​Bonta, a Democrat, ​said in a statement on ​Monday. “I want to remind Californians that customers of 23andMe ​can delete their private, ‌genetic data – no ​matter who owns ​it.”

The data breach exposed the genetic information of more than 855,000 Californians, according to the attorney general’s office.

23andMe agreed to pay $46.75m to victims of the 2023 data breach as part of its bankruptcy.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A California town’s beaches are washing away. Can its residents turn the tide?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and as Super El Niño rounds the corner, a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisis

San Clemente is one of southern California’s most picture-perfect beach towns – a capital of American surf culture since the 1950s. In two years, 2028 Olympic surfers will compete at Lower Trestles, a world-class surfing beach.

But the town’s longtime cultural and economic driver, its beaches, are now under threat. As pounding waves driven by late-summer storms in the Pacific devour chunks of the California coastline, some of San Clemente’s beaches are growing narrower, the sand increasingly eaten away.

Beach erosion has become a crisis all along the southern California shoreline this year, with towns from Dana Point and Long Beach to Malibu sustaining dramatic damage. But San Clemente is a particular flash point. It’s the place where the major regional train line, which carries $1bn in freight a year and is the nation’s second-busiest passenger line, runs right along the edge of the Pacific Ocean. Severe waves and high tides during big storms at the beginning of September forced the repeated closure of the tracks.

Experts say California’s current season of extreme weather is just getting started. “We’re in for a run of pretty exceptional erosion events if this Super El Niño develops as it’s expected to,” said Sean Vitousek, an oceanographer with the US Geological Survey (USGS).

As the potentially historic El Niño season overlaps with a massive surge of warm water called a Kelvin wave, residents worry it will leave coastal infrastructure in pieces, beachfront properties leveled and more beaches carved away to crumbling slivers of gravel and bare rock.

Donald Trump has continued to deny climate change as a “hoax”, “con job” or scam”. But in southern California, a historically conservative area, the effect of extreme weather events linked to the climate crisis have suddenly become very, very real.

“We’ve been anticipating rising sea levels 50 years from now,” said Hallie Jones, the mayor pro tem of Laguna Beach, California. “This summer proved that sea level rise is already here.”

On a hot, clear day, Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente beach restoration activist, took me to the state beach on the south side of town, where swimmers and sunbathers ambled over the major rail line’s tracks to perch on a very narrow strip of sand that descends steeply into the deep blue water.

“You can see, when it gets steep like this, then you’re just at a game of attrition,” Cosgrove told me. “It’s just a matter of time before the next big wave event will start moving and start taking some of this.”

Big storms at the beginning of September already saw the erosion of some of this coastline creep up to the train tracks. “Severe waves and high tides overtopped the tracks,” according to a spokesperson for the Orange County Transportation Authority (OCTA). The local commuter rail posted a video of sediment next to the tracks crumbling into the sea as waves slammed the shore.

After nearly a century of reliable service, the coastal rail line has been shut down seven times since 2021 for repairs after landslides and surging tides on stretches of the line in San Clemente and further south down the coast. Over the past five years, the closure times “have totaled more than one year”, an OCTA spokesperson confirmed.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

There’s no relief ahead. Once considered a gradual problem, coastal erosion is now being discussed more urgently, as the risk of California’s beaches simply disappearing, said Charles Lester, a former head of the California Coastal Commission who now leads an ocean policy center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. California scientists warned in 2023 that sea level rise sped up by the climate crisis threatens to erase between 25% and 75% of California’s beaches by 2100.

This is posing a massive challenge, particularly for leaders of smaller beachside towns whose appeal is built around their ocean access. Orange county, a collection of suburbs clustered between Los Angeles and San Diego, is famous as the birthplace of the Reagan Revolution. Today, the county is more politically purple than deep Republican red – more voters backed Kamala Harris than Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Some of its most famous beach towns, such as Newport Beach, remain Republican strongholds, favoring conservatism and as little government regulation as possible. But extreme weather and the growing threat to beaches is putting pressure even on Republican political orthodoxies.

Southern California’s wealthy coastal towns are used to breezier weather and lower temperatures than Los Angeles, or the scorching cities of the Inland Empire. But record-breaking heatwaves are changing that.

“It’s October 5 and it’s 90 degrees in Dana Point. Unless there’s Santa Ana [winds], it’s unheard of,” said John Gabbard, Dana Point’s Republican mayor. “The ocean temperature is high. There’s no wind. And that’s not happening just by happenstance. Nobody’s using the words ‘global warming’, but everybody is recognizing that it’s warmer and it continues to be warmer through the past few seasons than it’s ever been in the past.”

In San Clemente, where a majority of residents voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, Cosgrove, a retired IT executive, is advocating a radical move: he authored a ballot measure that will go before voters in November, asking local residents to voluntarily impose a 1% sales tax on themselves to fund beach restoration and wildfire prevention efforts. A large portion of that tax revenue would be dedicated to replacing what he estimates is the city’s deficit of 4m to 6m cubic yards of beach sand.

Nobody likes taxes, Cosgrove said, but voters need to face what he believes is the stark reality all along the California coast: if local residents don’t pay to protect public beaches from vanishing, it’s not clear that anyone else will.

Southern California’s wide, sandy beaches are not exactly a natural resource. Many of them were created or expanded with sand dredged up by major midcentury construction projects.

San Clemente’s beaches, for example, were fortified with an estimated 2m cubic yards of sand removed during the creation of Dana Point’s harbor in the late 1960s, Cosgrove said. “We’ve been living off that ever since,” he said.

Since those midcentury construction projects, further development and infrastructure, especially dams on California’s rivers, has blocked the flows of sediment that would naturally restock the beaches with sand, while competition for the available supply of dredged-up or trucked-in sand has grown more intense. This has made the erosion of California beach sand an ongoing issue for decades – but it’s a problem that is now escalating rapidly.

Much of California’s coastline development was completed during the state’s population boom from the 1940s to 1970s – years that happened to be an unusually “calm climate period” along the Pacific Ocean – “not many big El Niños, not a lot of storm damage”, Griggs, the coastline expert, said. “People built on the cliffs, they built on the bluffs, they built on the dunes.”

Since then, stronger El Niño seasons have returned – and this year threatens to be the worst on record.

Beach town residents such as Jones, the Laguna Beach mayor pro tem, who has lived there for much of her 48 years, are used to seeing sand migrate throughout the year. Beach sand is not a static amenity, but a complex system that can shift onshore and offshore, north and south. Scientists refer to each sand system as a “littoral cell”.

During winter storms, Jones said, Laguna’s beaches typically lose sand, but later storms tend to bring it back, a kind of natural restoration. What’s happening now, though, is “not business as usual”, Jones said.

Vitousek, the USGS oceanographer, said the intensity of this year’s coming tropical storms may disrupt beaches’ natural cycles: “You can get this thrashing, where the beach gets fully eroded on the south end, and then fully eroded on the north end,” he said. While beaches can sometimes recover “in a lot of cases, the damage is done. You’ve lost a beach. The waves are now breaking right on the infrastructure, causing damage.”

A few miles north of San Clemente, in Dana Point, the same ferocious Labor Day waves that paused train traffic through San Clemente ripped through a row of coastal residences, leaving 10 homes red-tagged as uninhabitable.

“The damage that we have seen this year has been extraordinary,” Gabbard, the mayor, said. He estimated there had been $33m in damage to private property, and another $25m in damage to the public beach.

Up and down the coast, lesser beach damage in early September served as a warning of what might be coming in the next months: a beachside parking lot was seriously damaged by waves in Laguna Beach, big sections of sand vanished around Balboa Pier in Newport Beach, and a sinkhole opened in the driveway of Nicholas Cage’s coastal mansion in Malibu.

In October, abnormally high tides flooded a low-lying neighborhood of Newport Beach, with local news outlets sharing footage of someone paddling on a surfboard through the streets. Huge waves damaged more homes in Long Beach. A dramatic crack in a cliffside bluff near Laguna Beach forced the continuing closure of part of the Pacific Coast Highway.

Though San Clemente’s Lower Trestles was not one of the hardest-hit beaches in early September, local news outlets have already begun speculating over whether future Super El Niño damage could cause problems for the beach as a major Olympic venue.

The most common short-term response to pounding waves that wash away local beaches and threaten beachside homes is to armor the shore with sea walls, revetments or simple piles of rocks. This has been a popular tactic, especially in southern California, where an estimated 38% of the coastline is now armored in some way. Half a century ago, in contrast, only 2.5% of California’s total coastline had armoring.

But armoring, though relatively fast and simple, has a hefty long-term cost. Environmentalists, beach-loving residents and California’s powerful coastal commission all warn that building walls to guard the coastline serves as a death knell to the beaches next to them.

Impermeable barriers block sediment from restocking the beach, while waves pounding on the barriers drag existing sand away, said Gary Griggs, a professor at University of California, Santa Cruz, who has been studying the California coastline for more than 50 years. In time, he said, any beach caught between the armoring and the sea disappears.

For beach restoration activists such as Cosgrove, a fully armored, fully beachless California shoreline is the future dystopia they are trying to avert. From San Clemente’s state beach, Cosgrove showed me what the future shoreline might look like, if coastal communities continue to respond to erosion with short-term crisis management of throwing down rocks and putting up walls. He pointed south towards Cypress Shores, one of San Clemente’s gated oceanfront communities. Beneath the clifftop homes, the waves pounded directly onto a revetment, a rocky barrier shielding the rail line and the foot of the cliffs. “They had a 200–ft beach,” Cosgrove said. “They had volleyball courts. They had barbecues. Now there’s no beach. It’s all armor.”

“If we never did sand replenishment, if we just don’t do anything at all, that revetment is the future of San Clemente,” Cosgrove told me. “From one end to the other. It may take 35 years to get there, but it will be that way.”

Environmentalists and some coastal experts say the only viable long-term strategy for the California shoreline is “managed retreat”. That means moving homes, roads and other infrastructure inland from the eroding coast – a response that requires huge amounts of planning, logistics and consensus building, and is about as popular with coastal homeowners and developers as one might expect.

“Most people don’t want to be managed, and most people don’t want to retreat,” said Griggs, the coastline expert. But, he added, “they’re not going to have a choice at some point”.

The centrist option, the one with the most support from across the political spectrum, is simply replenishing the sand on California’s eroded beaches – what Cosgrove is hoping to fund with his San Clemente ballot measure.

“It is a softer option than putting rock down, and it provides some more of that habitation and recreation space,” said Kelsey Ducklow, a coastal resilience coordinator at the California Coastal Commission.

Beaches are “the best natural buffer we have from waves”, Griggs said. “If the beach is narrowed or gone, the waves attack the cliffs directly.”

The problem is that hauling and dumping tons of sand on existing beaches is extremely costly and planning intensive – and not at all guaranteed to last, coastal experts said. Grigg described it as “a very, very temporary fix”.

“One big storm can remove hundreds of thousands of cubic feet [of sand],” Griggs said. At Torrey Pines beach in San Diego in 2001, he recalled, officials brought in 200,000 cubic yards of sand – equivalent to 20,000 dump truck loads, at a cost of more than $2m for that beach alone. “It stayed there for about eight months, during the spring and summer. Right around Thanksgiving, a storm hit, the waves came up, and [it] was gone overnight.”

In San Clemente, Cosgrove argued, the city’s beaches, which run between the protective arms of Dana Point and Cottons Point, are more sheltered, allowing new sand to stay within the system of beaches longer. An infusion of sand from 2024, placed with the help of the army corps of engineers, is still providing some cushion for the town’s beaches, he said. In the months he spent collecting signatures at the farmers’ market and local grocery store to get his sand-replenishment measure on the ballot, he heard widespread support for continuing to restock San Clemente beaches with new sand.

What people want to know, he said, is “Can someone else pay for this? Do we have to pay?” Residents want to know why the federal or state government isn’t funding beach replenishment with the taxes they already pay.

One might think that a state as known for government bureaucracy as California might have a statewide beach commission, or at least a state sand fund, to keep one of the state’s primary economic engines from disappearing. It does not. The California Coastal Commission has regulatory power up and down the shoreline and can provide small planning grants to local jurisdictions, but it does not have the kind of money necessary to fund big sand projects, a spokesperson said.

For that, Lester said, coastal cities usually need to go to the federal government and get a congressional appropriation for sand – a process that can easily take a decade, or even two, between when the state approves a replenishment plan and when federal money actually comes through.

In Dana Point, where a majority of voters also supported Trump in 2024, Gabbard is hoping the president will step in to help with emergency funds to help the coastal town’s continuing storm damage.

“Through back channels, I’ve been trying to get to the president to voice our concerns about, not just the homes themselves, but our beaches writ large, to make sure there are funds available to repair what we need to repair,” he said.

One of the many projects needed, he said, is to create a more natural buffer for future storm damage at Capistrano beach by building a sand berm – a single project estimated to cost $16m.

Even when federal funding is approved, cities are usually expected to provide matching funds for a big beach restoration project, Cosgrove said, which is why he thinks the most reliable option is for local residents to raise the money they need for beach restoration themselves, through a 10-year local sales tax. He said he is cautiously optimistic that San Clemente’s tax-skeptic voters will make an exception in November and vote to support wildfire prevention and the town’s beaches.

While the Orange county transportation administration recently pledged to expedite the placement of 690,000 cubic yards of sand to protect the crucial rail line through San Clemente, the timing of the project remains unclear, in part because the project will require “specialized marine dredging equipment”, and, of the US’s few existing machines, “many are committed to other projects months in advance”, an OCTA spokesperson said in a statement.

The state government is currently examining whether the rail line should simply be moved inland to a new location – a project already estimated to cost more than $5bn. The rail runs dangerously close to the ocean in both San Clemente and Del Mar, a town closer to San Diego.

Even if OCTA’s emergency sand restoration project in San Clemente is completed in a timely way, Cosgrove said, the amount of sand the agency has pledged to provide is far too little to restore all the city’s beaches.

In making his pitch to San Clemente voters, including on his Yes on Measure M website, Cosgrove doesn’t talk about the climate crisis, though he said he does see the role the warming ocean is playing in the extreme weather hitting California’s coast.

“I’m just messaging on stewardship and adding sand to our beaches,” he said. “This is the local issue that we’re facing. We can’t affect global climate change, but we can protect ourselves from it by nourishing our beaches. Having wide beaches is the best protection no matter what comes our way.”

Some residents have a less optimistic attitude about efforts to prevent further coastal damage. In San Clemente, Zhen Wu, a city council member, has opposed Cosgrove’s tax measure, telling the Associated Press: “Fighting mother nature is very expensive.”

On a hot October Friday, Kathy Ruiz, of Laguna Niguel, was sunbathing on a mostly-empty Aliso beach, not far from where construction equipment was repairing the Laguna beach parking lot damaged by early September storm surges.

“As far as people expecting the city to protect their homes, I don’t think that’s reasonable,” she said. “I think maybe they shouldn’t have built so close to the beach.”

Some residents want the government to build up sand berms to protect homes against the coming storms, Ruiz said, but she was skeptical.

“Nature is going to take its course,” Ruiz said. “I think all that stuff is in vain.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.

The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.

But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable.

Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers.

This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county: rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost.

“I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.”

Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies.

With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions, Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return.

What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community.

Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects.

It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in.

“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”

When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both.

Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee.

Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models.

“We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district.

“We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement.

While California has dozens of datacenters capable of cloud computing, streaming and internet searches, the state has scant facilities dedicated to AI. That’s because California is one of the most rigorous states when it comes to environmental permitting for energy and water-intensive facilities such as AI datacenters.

Major projects in California take an average of seven years to get completed, said Michael Thomas, the founder of Cleanview, which tracks datacenter development. For comparison, the average in Texas is about three years. Thomas said he had seen a surge of new players, like Rucci, get into AI datacenter development nationwide. These people, he said, were willing to take on the risk and find ways to speed up the process.

“Land and power have become so scarce at the scale that these big tech companies need,” Thomas said. So, if a developer can shorten the timeline, “a company like Google or Microsoft or Meta may be willing to pay you a huge premium … It’s potentially a way to make millions of dollars very quickly.”

Rucci is no stranger to taking on risk. He has owned a strip club, addiction treatment centers and dozens of accounting and real estate endeavors. In 2010, while operating the strip club, Go Go Cabaret, he was convicted on four counts of illegal liquor sales for which he had to serve a 30-day jail sentence. He was also charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, money laundering and promoting prostitution, but those charges were later dismissed. In 2019, California suspended his license to practice law for nearly three years.

He has also filed for corporate bankruptcy at least twice. The most recent time, in 2023, took place after the Department of Justice investigated one of his addiction treatment centers for alleged fraud, ending with a government seizure of $600,000 of assets. No criminal charges were filed, however, and that money was later returned with interest after Rucci sued the government to reclaim the seized funds.

Since zeroing in on Imperial county in 2024, Rucci has registered several new businesses related to the vast datacenter campus, from construction and energy supply to ongoing operations. The umbrella company for his project is an LLC called Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). Rucci says the facility will bring in more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30m in annual tax revenue. It will also include an electrical substation, on-site battery energy storage and more than 130 methane-gas-fueled generators, according to an application submitted to the county planning department.

Rucci said his diverse experience was well-suited for such a complicated project. “That doesn’t mean that my background isn’t colorful,” he said. “I’ve challenged cities. I fought the federal government. I’ve done a lot of stuff. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t know how to process this and get it through.”

At first, Leal had no clue that the dusty 75 acres of land across the street from his house had been bought by a developer. It wasn’t until the day before Thanksgiving last year when he found a colorful flyer hanging from his door that his world began to swirl around him. The flyer mapped out the huge project and warned that construction was moving forward without requiring the state’s usual environmental review.

Leal began scanning the internet, and what he found shocked him. His back fence was all that separated his home from Rucci’s property. While Leal lived in Imperial city, the datacenter would fall just outside city limits on unincorporated county land. It was clear that living next to this facility would permanently change the quiet life he and his wife had envisioned when they moved there some 20 years earlier.

“When we bought that house, we planned for it to be the house where we would retire, where our kids would grow up and return when they visit,” Leal said. “The quality of life of anybody living half a mile from the datacenter will be affected.”

He started texting his neighbors that same day. As word spread, people began to organize, holding meetings and rallies against the datacenter proposal. Within months, close to 3,500 people would sign a petition opposing the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla, who represents the district, would sound the alarm, introducing a series of bills aimed at datacenters.

As AI datacenters have popped up around the world, they’ve come under scrutiny for being extremely resource-intensive. A query through chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini needs nearly 10 times as much electricity as a typical internet search, and that number can increase for more complicated prompts. Because supercomputers run hot, they typically need extensive water-cooling systems.

Imperial county is a critical habitat for wildlife like the desert pupfish, which is listed as an endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act and swims through agricultural drains and canals, much like one that crosses Rucci’s property. Other desert animals of concern include the flat-tailed horned lizard, yellow-breasted chat and burrowing owls.

As Leal got more involved in the datacenter fight, he met other concerned residents, like Christopher Scurries. Scurries lives nearby and is a music teacher at Imperial high school. He said he was worried about datacenter noise, what’s known as a constant low hum. “I’ll definitely hear when I’m here in my house,” he said. Scurries and his wife moved to the area in 2017 so they could afford a home. Now with a two-year-old daughter, his previously pleasant life feels uncertain in the shadow of the datacenter.

It’s testament to a long-simmering sentiment in this corner of the Sonoran desert, where pollutants from agriculture and industry, along with poverty, have long taken an undue toll. One in five adults is unemployed in the region and the poverty rate, at close to 20%, is the highest in California.

“The benefits these structures may bring into a community – the jobs, tax revenue, even the infrastructure improvements – may feel uncertain or uneven compared to the scale of the impact,” said Carla Walker, the US director of environmental justice and equity at the research organization World Resources Institute. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price.”

For Jacob Rodriguez, who was born and raised in the area, who pays the price has been top of mind. “It’s an existential threat,” he said of the datacenter project, noting that residents had long dealt with pollution and dwindling water supplies. “The respiratory problems and the air quality here are already abysmal … eventually, indirectly, this will cost lives.”

By March, tensions between Rucci and the community had reached a boiling point. At an Imperial county board of supervisors meeting, dozens of residents, including Leal and Scurries, packed into the chambers for a public feedback session. As Rucci stood at the lectern, trying to present his more than 100 slides on the project, the crowd steadily chanted “no datacenters” and waved “not in my backyard” signs. It got so raucous that Rucci, the main speaker on the schedule, left the meeting early.

As he walked out of the building, protesters yelled “Fuera, Rucci, fuera” (“leave” in Spanish). Visibly fed up, Rucci unexpectedly approached a person screaming through a bullhorn and roared in their face.

By this point, the project was at the center of a heated legal battle. The city of Imperial had sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental reviews when it approved the datacenter (the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club later joined on). Rucci, in turn, counter-sued in federal court on behalf of his company IVCM, alleging the city carried out a “bad-faith campaign of administrative obstruction and targeted retaliation”.

He then went on to sue an anti-datacenter activist named Jake Tison, the Comité Cívico del Valle non-profit, and its executive director, Luis Olmedo, and the local public-media news station KPBS and one of its reporters, Kori Suzuki, for defamation. Those three defamation suits were dismissed. Rucci has appealed in the cases against KPBS and Comité Cívico del Valle and is working to reverse the ruling on Tison.

“Look, I’m not here to run for Miss America or Mr America,” Rucci said. “I’m here to do a datacenter.”

Rucci, on behalf of IVCM, also sued the local utility, the Imperial irrigation district, for rejecting an application for water to cool the datacenter. The utility’s sole source of water is the drought-stricken Colorado River. The AI facility would need about 750,000 gallons of water a day, according to Rucci.

He says the water the datacenter would use is equivalent to a 160-acre farm, of which there are several in the area. The utility’s officials, however, voiced concerns about how the project would affect residents. Karin Euenio, one of the utility’s directors, wrote in an op-ed: “I believe it is my duty to speak up when a proposal raises serious concerns about ratepayers, reliability, and community wellbeing.”

The tumult continued through the spring and summer, with Rucci’s IVCM spending $30,000 in a campaign to back his company spokesperson, Carlos Duran, to fill the seat of one of the utility district’s directors. He lost.

For its part, the community instigated its own political organizing efforts with a recall campaign of Peggy Price, the chair of Imperial county’s board of supervisors who has been supportive of the datacenter. That campaign is ongoing.

While things had been looking good for Rucci after he got county approval for the project in April, it took a drastic turn over the last month. The judge presiding over the city’s lawsuit ruled Rucci must go back to square one for the entire approval process. That means before breaking ground, the datacenter must clear lengthy environmental reviews to assess its impact on the power grid, water supply and emissions.

Alene Taber, a lawyer representing Imperial, said these reviews could take a year or more and that alternative locations for the datacenter would have to be taken into consideration. She said it was meaningful “that there [will be] a transparent, public, environmental process”.

Rucci, however, said he was not deterred and is going to challenge the judge’s ruling. “It’ll be just a matter of time,” he said. “I’m not going away.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Six homes burned and two firefighters injured in fast-moving California wildfire
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
About 6,000 homes under evacuation, affecting 16,000 residents in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano

At least six homes burned and two firefighters were injured after a fast-moving wildfire blazed through parts of southern California on Friday.

Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries from the Norte fire, officials said.

“As reported yesterday, we can confirm that six homes have been destroyed or damaged, there have been two firefighter injuries, and the cause is still under investigation,” an Orange County Fire Authority (OCFA) official shared in a statement via social media Saturday morning.

TJ McGovern, the OCFA chief, also confirmed, in a press conference Friday, that there have been no reports of resident injuries or deaths thus far.

McGovern attributed the severity of the wildfires to natural forces, such as weather and wind.

“Due to weather and topography, this fire moved fast. This was a wind-driven event,” McGovern said.

With wind gusts ranging from 50-70mph (80-110km/h), as of Saturday morning, the fire had spread to 570 acres (230 hectares) and was 5% contained, after OCFA crews worked throughout the night by land and air to aggressively attack the fire and strengthen containment lines.

The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano.

It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast.

By Friday night, about 6,000 homes were under mandatory evacuation, affecting 16,000 residents. An evacuation shelter had opened in each city.

According to the National Weather Service, the Santa Ana winds would linger through Saturday, and the potential for extreme fire behavior and rapid spread could still rise.

To help prevent utility equipment from sparking new blazes, in northern California, nearly 62,000 customers in 26 counties had their electricity proactively turned off on Wednesday night, according to Pacific Gas and Electric Company.

More than 118,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.

Destructive conditions fueled by a potentially historic El Niño brewing in the Pacific will continue to mount through the end of this year and into next.

But on the heels of the recent storm surge that battered the California coast, the weather whiplash has left residents reeling.

The NWS’s red flag warning for parts of southern California is in effect through Saturday night.

Just north of San Clemente, a wildfire dubbed the Henderson fire had burned 3,132 acres across parts of San Diego and was at 35% containment, according to Cal Fire.

Fire crews responded to the Henderson fire just before 2pm Thursday leading to the closure of Interstate 5.

Friday evening, the freeway closure was fully lifted, and at press time there were no reported injuries. The cause of the fire remains unknown and under investigation.

The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win against Villarreal
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Andoni Iraola and Iñigo Pérez parked their long and close friendship in the buildup to the Champions League duel between two old Athletic Bilbao teammates. They will have a humdinger of a contest to dissect when communications are restored. Liverpool, driven by Alexis Mac Allister and ignited by Rio Ngumoha, recovered from two goals down against Villarreal to maintain their 100% record in the competition in emphatic style.

Mac Allister struck twice as Liverpool fought back from a tepid start to record a third successive win in all competitions. They were given a scare when Tani Oluwaseyi volleyed in a late third for Villarreal but were well deserving of their latest impressive result.

The regular phone calls between Iraola and Pérez had eased off as their first competitive confrontation as coaches approached. Iraola could have advised his close friend to bring a coat had they kept in touch. It had rained incessantly in Liverpool all day yet the Villarreal head coach opted for a short-sleeved polo shirt on the touchline. A brave move, although he would have been warmed by his team’s potent start against a much-changed host.

Liverpool’s expensive attacking trio of Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola were all on the bench as Iraola made six changes to the side that beat Brentford on Saturday. A fourth game in 10 days explained the omissions of Wirtz and Barcola, who had featured heavily in the previous three, while Isak’s workload was being carefully managed after his recent thigh injury. The rotation resulted in a second successive Champions League start for Trey Nyoni and Ryan Gravenberch shifting forward into Wirtz’s number ten role.

Iraola’s rejigged team did not have time to find their rhythm before falling behind. An error-strewn start by Van Dijk was responsible, and also in keeping with a ponderous opening half hour from Liverpool in which Villarreal passed their way around Anfield with style and precious little resistance.

The Liverpool captain presented Georges Mikautadze with an opportunity as early as the second minute when he misjudged a long clearance out of defence by Renato Veiga. Van Dijk’s poor touch almost released the Georgia international striker through on goal but Jérémy Jacquet was across quickly to close off that route. Van Dijk’s second slip followed moments later, and this time there was no reprieve. The defender attempted to head another Veiga long ball back into the safe arms of Alisson. He found Mikautadze instead and Villarreal’s number nine pounced expertly, controlling well before rolling the ball under the Liverpool keeper. There were apologies all round from Van Dijk.

Villarreal doubled their lead with a goal that encapsulated the start made by both teams – the visitors passing their way through Liverpool’s midfield and picking holes in their high defensive line, with the home side slow to react. Pape Gueye, Alberto Moleiro and Nathan Saliba all combined to send their rampaging left back, Sergi Cardona, clear of the Liverpool backline. Played onside by Kostas Tsimikas, the full-back beat Alisson with a finish a striker would have been happy with.

Cardona’s defending was much less impressive as Liverpool, stung more by their own performance than the groans of the Anfield crowd, clawed their way back into the contest before half-time. The recovery commenced when Mac Allister rose superbly to meet a Tsimikas corner and flicked an unstoppable header into the unguarded side of Peter Gulacsi’s goal. The former Liverpool keeper could only stand and admire the midfielder’s header, while asking where a Villarreal challenge was.

Villarreal had bigger questions to answer when their once comfortable lead vanished entirely with the final kick of the first half. The visitors had dealt with another corner from Tsimikas when Rio Ngumoha gathered possession and clipped a cross towards the far post. Cardona checked his surroundings, then inexplicably let the ball bounce behind him. And right into the spot where Ronald Araújo was lurking. The on-loan defender headed home for the second successive week in the Champions League and celebrated with a mass pile-on with fans in the Anfield Road Stand.

Araújo failed to appear for the second half as Iraola introduced Wirtz and moved Gravenberch once again, this time to right back. The Liverpool head coach must have been sorely tempted to shake things up more, such was the paucity of his team’s first half display, but his half-time switch and demands sufficed. Liverpool improved vastly after the restart with Ngumoha and Wirtz a constant threat. Pérez’s substitutions were less impactful and the former Newcastle forward Ayoze Pérez was the object of his ire on several occasions.

Ngumoha took the acclaim of the Kop after creating Mac Allister’s second of the night with a sparkling run down the right. It was some one-two that brought Liverpool the lead. Mac Allister floated a pass out to the 18-year-old winger, whose first touch brought the ball under control and took him away from Cardona in the same movement. He then left the substitute Juan Foyth in his wake before pulling back a pass from the byline for the incoming midfielder to smash a shot in off the underside of Gulacsi’s crossbar.

Wirtz completed the comeback, continuing his own recent improvement, after Tsimikas and Cody Gakpo had combined to create space for the playmaker inside the area. The Germany international drilled a clinical left-foot finish inside the Villarreal keeper’s far corner.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Foden hat-trick helps Manchester City cut through noise and crush AEK Athens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Enzo Maresca has called for Manchester City to make their own noise on the pitch to drown out the cacophony surrounding them but maybe a quiet night at the Etihad Stadium was what they needed all along. AEK Athens were easily dispatched in a businesslike manner, as Phil Foden announced his return to form with a hat-trick to get City’s Champions League campaign back on track after being pummelled by Paris Saint-Germain.

The match was uneven throughout as Foden shone on the wing and later down the middle, with goals from Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki helping to ease City to victory in front of half-full stands. Stavros Pilios’s consolation was more a reward for the boisterous fans in yellow and black than for the overall efforts of the visitors.

Enzo Maresca took the calculated risk of eight changes from the win over Ipswich, although that did mean a return to the starting lineup for Enzo Fernández and Elliot Anderson while Erling Haaland was left on the bench. His replacement, with senior options lacking, was the 17-year-old academy graduate, Floyd Samba, whose only other senior football came in a Carabao Cup win against Norwich, when he scored twice on debut.

The game had not captured the imagination with the stands having huge gaps of blue, which is understandable amid the constant churn of fixtures for City and the cost of following the club. AEK was seen by many fans as a game that could be missed, in expectation of a simple victory over a team lacking global superstars. The visiting supporters were far more animated, filling a corner of the ground over three tiers where they created a party from two hours before kick-off.

Inspiration was required from those on the pitch with the home faithful subdued, which was provided by Fernández clipping a free-kick on to the bar and Anderson following up to whack the rebound into an empty net in the 12th minute. The celebrations lacked enthusiasm, acknowledged with a nod of approval.

AEK had no desire to capitulate and created some promising moves without ever threatening the City box, lacking quality when it mattered most. The Greek side had half of the possession in the opening quarter but the hosts, although not at their best, turned on the style when required, going from static to full steam in seconds to create chances.

The Champions League debutant Allan was City’s most entertaining offering, providing direct running and skill on the left wing. The Brazilian was a menace and almost marked his second home appearance with a goal but his vicious shot clipped the bar and flew into the stands. With seven matches in 21 days for City, games like this gave an opportunity for fringe players to impress and Allan was eager to make his mark.

City were able to take control, passing the ball around with ease and holding AEK at arm’s length, while Foden and Rayan Cherki tried to work their fleet-footed magic in tight spaces. Eventually the calmness in the final third was rewarded when Foden finished after neat work on the right from Rico Lewis, as the two academy products combined. The full-back has struggled for minutes in recent times and almost left the club 16 months ago but showed he can provide something as an attacking threat from defence.

With City comfortable, complacency kicked in and Abdukodir Khusanov reflected the crowd by drifting off, giving Zini the chance to turn him and slip a pass into Stavros Pilios who thrashed the ball across Gianluigi Donnarumma. The AEK fans erupted, while their counterparts pondered how City had been dragged back into a fight, having previously been impenetrable.

Natural order was restored by Cherki, a neat trick inside the box and a precise shot into the corner did the rest. It was an occasion for the maverick Frenchman to be a leader, making the difference in critical moments and he offered up evidence of his capabilities with the finish, creating breathing space in the process.

If the plan was to test life without Haaland, the loss of Antoine Semenyo to injury for eight weeks created a problem for Maresca. Samba’s deployment ranked somewhere between plan C and D but the teenager was an adept decoy, allowing the more experienced around him to show off their repertoire. Samba acquitted himself well but whether he is a suitable replacement for the Norwegian will remain unknown until City face more competitive opposition.

City were starting to showboat as AEK realised resistance was futile. Cherki knocked it long for Lewis to control into the path of Foden, who provided a sublime first-time finish into the top corner from the edge of the box. The exceptional goals were racking up on what felt like an otherwise mundane night.

On a positive night for City’s academy, Ryan McAidoo came off the bench to send in a perfect cross for Foden to complete his treble with a striker’s instinct, earning the biggest cheer of the night. Foden scored his first goal since mid-December at the weekend but the confidence is clearly flooding back to a player who has spent too long watching on from the sidelines, especially considering the talent he possesses.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Albanian Student Strikes Spur a Political Crisis
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
A new round of protests against the ruling party’s corruption has Prime Minister Edi Rama giving cops bonuses to crack down on dissent.

For the past week, students in the Albanian capital of Tirana have been on strike—an action that’s spurred major clashes with police and widespread damage to government buildings and public property. In response, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has sought to step up the government crackdown, offering security forces extra money to suppress the worst political crisis of his 13 years in office.

The specter of a more intensive backlash does nothing to address the issues that sent Albanian students into the streets: increased education fees, poor school conditions, and a lengthy list of government corruption scandals, including the possibly illegal sale of land to Jared Kushner for luxury property development. In lieu of endorsing reforms on all these issues, Rama chose violence.

The latest turn in Albanian protest politics will likely just ratchet up the mood of growing frustration among dissenters. For 130 days this summer, Tirana saw a wave of peaceful protests against Rama’s approval of the Kushner-backed resort project—a boondoggle that detractors have argued only benefits powerful oligarchs close to Rama’s government.

But what happened last week took everyone by surprise. The Albanian student union called for school strikes and planned a series of demonstrations at the Education Ministry in central Tirana. The protests kept growing, and eventually a handful of black-masked provocateurs began tearing out CCTV cameras and stoplights in the city center. The confrontation escalated from there: Restive protesters threw rocks, exploded fireworks, and burned dumpsters. The cops responded with tear gas, water cannons, and baton beatings. Not surprisingly, the response pushed more demonstrators into anger.

Toward the end of the week, things got ugly. Demonstrations and vandalism paralyzed the city; banks, government ministries, police stations, and Rama’s political party headquarters were battered and burned by bricks and Molotov cocktails. A pattern emerged: Daytime protests mixed peaceful protesters with teenage Albanians throwing and breaking things; and nightfall brought pitched street battles between cops and more aggressive, older, and angrier crowds. Now cars and buildings were burning—and in one fracas with protesters, a cop was briefly set aflame.

By Sunday night, downtown Tirana scarcely had any stoplights, streetlights, bus stops, or dumpsters that weren’t damaged. Streets were covered with rocks, broken glass, and smoke, while clouds of tear gas besieged rioters and confused tourists. At least 100 protesters and 50 police have been treated for injuries, and dozens of protesters have been hospitalized or arrested.

“You cannot negotiate with this,” said Rama, displaying a piece of broken concrete at a Monday meeting with police officers. “The moment the state negotiates with this, it has fallen.”

In the closed meeting—Rama has limited public appearances since the protests began in June—the president said he was willing to discuss complaints about his government’s track record. But he stressed that he wouldn’t entertain the demands of protest leaders.

“Dialogue at any hour, on any day, anywhere, with anyone, except the political forces behind the violence that refuse to distance themselves from it,” he said. Given how long Albanians have been demonstrating against his government—and how widespread the protests have grown—Rama is essentially saying he’ll only negotiate with elites who are already likely to be in accord with his government anyway. Then came his bid to keep the security forces in crackdown mode: a pledge of across-the-board bumps in salary and a one-time bonus of about $2,800 to cops clashing with rioters. Most protesters saw the offer as a flagrant bribe designed to shore up his increasingly unpopular government.

“Rama doesn’t have the money to educate students because politicians steal public funds and he sells our land to his friends and foreigners without debate,” said Agim, a 22-year-old barista and student who comes out to protest when his schedule permits. “But somehow he’s got millions of euros to bribe the police to protect him.”

Despite Rama’s resounding election victory last year over opposition leader Sali Berisha, any residual sense of his governing under a popular mandate has succumbed to the overt corruption of his regime—and his refusal to confront popular dissent is only compounding his isolation from the struggles of ordinary Albanians.

And amid conditions of government impunity and corruption, public cynicism mounts. “Berisha and Rama are seen in the same light,” said a local journalist who covers crime and corruption, and asked not to be named because of mounting threats against regime opponents. “They compete with each other to control a rotten system for their gain and to repay their oligarch backers and the cocaine mafia that controls Albania’s economy. There’s no good guys on either side. But one bad guy [Rama] is more palatable to the European Union.”

In Albania’s relatively free press and political system, overt political repression is rare. But the journalist is far from alone in worrying about a crackdown. Lorenzo, a 24-year-old waiter and protester, explains that face masks and avoiding arrest are crucial.

“If the police arrest you, you can lose any scholarship or government job,” he said. “My mother is a nurse at a government hospital in Korča. If my face is photographed and the police identify me, she could lose her job. They’re threatening our families.”

In the 1990s, after Albania broke free from a brutal communist regime that ruled for 45 years, crushing dissent and immiserating the populace, the country fell into chaotic violence. Local gangs, former security commanders, and an influential cohort of organized crime bosses effectively lorded over the streets until peacekeepers from nearby Italy helped restore government control in 1999.

From that low point, Albania was able to transition into a fairly calm, peaceful, and democratic state, even as its economy floundered. As the government managed to deliver basic services, and secure basic freedom of movement and speech, street crime also abated, and a small but growing tourist economy took hold, seeking to exploit the country’s pristine beaches and stunning mountain ranges.

After Rama came to power in 2013, he was able to leverage Albania’s more stable footing into an investment-friendly economic agenda. He also embarked on the long path to Albania’s admission to the EU in 2030—a plan that most citizens of this former pariah state eagerly support.

Yet Rama’s reputation as a competent technocratic reformer was short-lived. Despite Albania’s progress toward a more open society, the country has never managed to break the feudal control of its economy by powerful families and clans. Corruption moved behind closed doors as officials and oligarchs divided public funds among them, and employed bribes to secure overpriced government contracts. The economy, particularly for young people, completely stagnated, leading to an exodus over the last decade of at least a half a million Albanians out of a total population of just under 3 million.

Albanian crime lords, meanwhile, acquired a major interest in Europe’s lucrative cocaine trade. Albanians played an outsize role in transporting cocaine from South America to ports in Europe, which they then leveraged into control of much of the wholesale trade across Europe. Albanian gangsters ran much of the traffic in cocaine and heroin in the United Kingdom after waging a bloody gang war across London to drive out rival English and Kurdish gangs.

The proceeds and criminal fallout of this drug coup haven’t directly affected life in the Albanian homeland—most Albanians can’t afford cocaine, and the local marijuana trade is peaceful enough. But the country is plagued with rampant money laundering, as Albanian drug lords seek to transform billions in cocaine-related revenue into bank accounts and legal assets.

This means that there’s been a paper boom in the construction of restaurants, business, and apartments and resorts across the country. Tirana’s under a massive construction boom, with cocaine money springing for an estimated 12,000 new luxury apartment units that few Albanians can afford.

If Tirana were able to harness all the incoming drug money into something like a viable development plan, Rama might have been able to purchase a measure of social peace and stability. But this spending and development hasn’t led to better jobs or increased public funding of basic services. Instead, Albanians are facing the major signs of oligarch-bred inequality: soaring housing prices, expensive bars and restaurants that clearly lose money, and the surreal sight of twentysomething guys with Manchester and London accents driving Bentleys around Western Europe’s poorest capital—all in the shadow of luxury apartment towers that no reasonable person expects to be inhabited.

Albanian students aren’t dumb; the corruption and predation of Rama’s regime have greatly disillusioned the rising generation of Albanians. The luckiest among them have emigrated to other European countries, settling in the UK, Belgium, Netherlands, Germany, Greece, and Switzerland to work ordinary jobs that offer a future; the country’s émigré population is well into the hundreds of thousands. A 24-year-old truck driver named Luisi who’s turned out for the protests says he’s also thinking of leaving the country for Malmo, Sweden, where a cousin of his lives—and where Balkan organized crime has established a major hub. Luisi now supplements his modest $600-a-month salary by selling small amounts of marijuana and cocaine in clubs that he can’t afford to visit unless he’s working. His cousin assures him that “there’s work and I can make a lot of money.”

When I ask him what his cousin does, Luisi laughs. “He’s a gangster bro, he wants me to come help him. I don’t know if I should. But I’ll never get a good job or buy a house in Albania.”

Luisi then starts to interview me: “How much does a commercial truck driver get paid in America? I don’t want to be a gangster with my cousin, but I can’t stay here.”

Mitchell Prothero has covered international crime, terrorism, intelligence, and security issues from the Middle East and Europe for over two decades. Previously Iraq bureau chief for McClatchy Newspapers, he’s written about security and terrorism in Europe for BuzzFeed News and as a senior writer for Vice World News. He’s currently based in Tirana, Albania.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Why Calling Anti-Trans Hate a “Distraction” Is So Troubling
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
It’s a familiar line in the midterms: Anti-trans attacks are a “distraction” from “kitchen-table” issues. That sends a chilling message about whose rights are worth fighting for.

Over the past decade, open bigotry against immigrants, trans people, Muslims, and vulnerable communities of all kinds—has moved even more firmly to the center of US politics. At the same time, many people trying to combat the forces churning up this hate have settled on a familiar line: that the attacks on these groups are a political “distraction” from the “kitchen-table” issues facing Americans. It’s become such a common refrain that a recent poll indicated a majority of US adults endorse it. And it’s a line being used over and over again by Democratic candidates throughout this year’s midterms.

It’s easy to see why this framing has taken hold. By painting inflammatory positions as desperate attempts to evade discussion, proponents hope to disarm them. The conventional wisdom is that somewhere in the imagination of the average voter, there are core issues that really matter—usually to do with the cost of living. These, they contest, should be the rightful focus of political debate.

But embedded in this taxonomy of “distractions” and “core issues” is a series of assumptions about whose opinion matters in an election, and more importantly, whose rights are worth fighting for. Many of us in the groups being most commonly targeted by the far right are left to wonder if this dogmatic pursuit of the least controversial platform is less a strategy than a cultivated apathy—or, worse, whether our ostensible allies ever cared for us at all if it is so easy to cast us aside.

I have lost count of how many times I’ve left work over the past five years only to realize one push notification later that I had more rights in the morning than I did in the afternoon. The week after Trump’s passport executive order, I kept forgetting to breathe. While social media swirled with speculation about what this was meant to distract the public away from, visions of a grim future unspooled in my head. When it feels like your world is ending and the most people can be bothered to say about it is that something actually important must be happening somewhere else, the clear message is that what is happening to you is a second-tier issue—that you don’t really count.

The distraction discourse also doesn’t account for what happens when politicians supposedly on the “good” side embrace bigotry themselves. Is the response to, say, the recent decision by South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews to release an anti-trans ad to dismiss it as a distraction—or to ignore it entirely? This wasn’t just a rhetorical shift. This was an otherwise progressive politician being dragged into the realm of authoritarian prejudice—the kind of choice that has potentially life-altering consequences for those of us who live here under the bus. Shouldn’t that matter?

On a practical level, the distraction strategy has also failed Democrats repeatedly. In 2024, strategists convinced Democrats to court the center exclusively. Despite retroactive claims to the contrary, no overtures to pro-trans policy were made by the Harris campaign. Her answer on the question of protecting gender-affirming care was middling. Her foreign policy on Palestine was hawkish. Rather than attack xenophobia at its roots, she bragged that her policy on immigration in many ways would be harsher than Trump’s. None of us need to be reminded that she lost that election decisively. Those she was cynically attempting to court were mostly unpersuaded, while those of us whose lives were determined by concessions made in pursuit of the biggest possible tent were edged out of what we’re told is our only political home.

Yet, in the aftermath, those who had crafted this approach claimed inexplicably that the opposite had happened—that Harris had lost because she had pandered too much to the left. Today, while Democrats pivot past an imaginary center towards the right, Republicans continue their pursuit of minority groups undaunted. If it is a distraction for Democratic politicians, it appears to be a permanent cornerstone for the GOP.

Moreover, claims to “distraction” fail to understand how reactionary politics work. Cultural issues, broadly speaking, are used to glue together value systems in the service of creating a larger, unified voting base. Project 2025 was particularly terrifying because, however small and insignificant each of those individual positions may have appeared on their own, together they created a cohesive framework governing every aspect of life. Xenophobia, gender policing, and the criminalization of reproductive freedoms are animating principles of fascism. They give life to it.

Today’s campaigns are light on facts and heavy on emotional appeals. It matters that both of Trump’s terms were won by appealing to emotions while Democratic candidates focused on pragmatics. Emotional appeals are so central to the conservative platform that more money has been poured into anti-trans advertising than any other issue, and those expenditures show no signs of slowing down. They believe they’ve struck gold, in part because they do so in the absence of much opposition.

The fact that these ads do not appear to be moving the immediate political needle—Republicans are significantly underperforming in advance of next month’s elections, after all—doesn’t negate the impact they have had, particularly when it comes to enforcing near-total silence or, worse, active complicity from Democrats toward the attacks on trans people. As Democrats continue to fold on trans rights, they have allowed far-right actors to cement anti-trans and anti-immigrant animus into national policy.

Research suggests that rather than appear more reasonable, parties who cave on contested territory only convince the general public that their opposition to those parties was correct. There is no ground the party can cede that will satiate fascism, and a party that espouses equality but fails to defend it is morally hollow.

While it’s true that bombast historically has been the refuge of desperate politicians, many of them went on to reshape the world in their own brutal but otherwise perfunctory images. History’s villains clearly show it is possible to galvanize large swaths of the public through hate in order to seize and maintain power.

When Trump first declared that he would “secure the border” in 2015 by erecting an enormous wall across the entire southern US border, this too was labeled a distraction even well into 2019—an unserious proposal to mask the absence of cogent policy. Democrats had already shown themselves to be quite committed to border warfare, with former President Obama having escalated deportations during his two terms far above his predecessor. But building a wall was exactly what Trump ultimately did. As migrants drown trying to survive concertina wire and gunfire from newly erected border fortifications, we must concede that this was not merely a performance. Trump’s anti-immigrant policies have metastasized. Eight years after his initial promise to build that wall, Trump’s running mate made the astonishing claim that Middle America was besieged with immigrants eating the pets of their neighbors. That man is now vice president.

A plurality of voters do not draw such a careful division between pragmatic policies and those rooted in emotional appeal. The attention violent crime is given vastly outweighs the impact it has on the average voter. The most violent crimes—those involving high-capacity firearms—remain fundamentally unaddressed. Meanwhile, thinly veiled anti-Black racism couched in “law and order” rhetoric has pushed US policy ever rightward for 40 years.

Even if we accept that at one point the issues in question had once been chosen to “distract”, they became intimately woven into core policies of the GOP. They are part and parcel of every minute of Fox News. There is historical precedent. When abortion, homophobia, and anti-feminism were centralized as pillars of the conservative platform during the “Moral Majority” in 1979, it may not have been a driving force behind American politics quite yet. But soon it was, and it laid the ground for the modern far right to germinate and take root.

These issues weren’t used to draw attention away from the policy failures the party had championed. They were instead used to make these more enticing, to appeal to a broader audience and signal the new direction of conservative policy. They harnessed the anger of conservatives towards the anti-war movement, the rise of feminism, and the gathering successes of the civil rights movement, and directed this energy toward institutional capture. Policing bodies, and specifically reproduction, was a brass ring to hold out to those who felt they had otherwise lost control of their lives. As church-aligned politicians embraced anti-abortion policies to build voter power, these policies began to impact how those voters saw not only the ballot but the church itself. A feedback loop was created, reshaping the modern conservative movement less toward small government, more toward the promise of a bulwark against Gomorrah.

At the point at which every major university has had its curriculum reconfigured to comport with the approved national history, where major landmarks have been taken down, renamed or otherwise defaced to obscure painful facets of our history, where gender policing has been enshrined by executive order down to middle school soccer games, is it still distraction or does it yet count as policy? Facing these policies head-on, not as a passing phase but an entrenchment of authoritarianism, is an existential imperative. Marginalized communities whose lives are increasingly imperiled by this entrenchment cannot wait. While it will be a very long time before any of us can breathe deeply again, a bold and affirmative defense of human rights is necessary for our survival.

Jessica Kant is a writer and licensed independent clinical social worker based in Boston.
